web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Syllabus Overview
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Organisation of English K–10

The organisation of outcomes and content for English K–10 highlights the role and connection that Understanding Texts and Creating Texts have across all areas of English. The organisation of outcomes and content reflects the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to learn, including the study of a wide range of literature.

The knowledge, understanding and skills described in the outcomes and content of each focus area provide a basis for students to successfully progress to the next stage of learning. Focus areas should not be interpreted as hierarchical or time bound, as instructional priorities will be informed by learner needs. Across a stage of learning all focus areas need to be taught.

K–2 focus areas

The focus areas for each stage support students’ growing knowledge and understanding in the areas of:

  • Oral language and communication
  • Vocabulary
  • Phonological awareness
  • Print conventions
  • Phonic knowledge
  • Reading fluency
  • Reading comprehension
  • Creating written texts
  • Spelling
  • Handwriting
  • Understanding and responding to literature
3–6 focus areas

The focus areas for each stage support students’ growing knowledge and understanding in the areas of:

  • Oral language and communication
  • Vocabulary
  • Reading fluency
  • Reading comprehension
  • Creating written texts
  • Spelling
  • Handwriting and digital transcription
  • Understanding and responding to literature

In English K–6, the importance of strong foundations in the early years across oral language, reading and writing is highlighted. The organisation of the syllabus supports the development of early literacy knowledge and skills, while continuing to acknowledge the importance of learning about and enjoying literature.

Evidence highlights the importance of oral language, reading and writing. Oral language can include spoken, nonverbal, symbolic and gestural forms. This includes Auslan, which fulfils the same function as oral language in meeting the communication and language development needs of students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing.

7–10 focus areas

The focus areas for each stage support students’ growing knowledge and understanding in the areas of:

  • Reading, viewing and listening to texts
  • Understanding and responding to texts
  • Expressing ideas and composing texts

English 7–10 builds on the foundational skills developed in the earlier years to support the growing knowledge, understanding and skills in the areas of Reading, viewing and listening to texts, Understanding and responding to texts and Expressing ideas and composing text.

Image long description: The 3 focus areas of the English 7–10 Syllabus: Reading, viewing and listening to texts; Understanding and responding to texts; and Expressing ideas and composing texts. The first focus area is surrounded by a rectangular box titled Understanding texts. The third focus area is surrounded by a rectangular box titled Composing texts. The second focus area is elongated, so as to be included in both rectangular boxes.

Text requirements

Engaging with texts is central to the study of English.

For English 7–10 Text requirements see the course description.

Access content points K–6

Life Skills outcomes and content

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

Balance of content

Working at different stages

Students who are new to learning English may understand concepts, themes and ideas appropriate to higher stages of learning. However, teachers may need to provide additional explicit teaching of content that will support students' language learning and enable them to demonstrate their understandings.

For example:

  • Some students in Early Stage 1 could be working on the Stage 1 Vocabulary outcome while also working on Early Stage 1 Phonic Knowledge
  • In Stage 2 or Stage 3, some students may not have learnt initial and extended phonic knowledge and will need explicit phonics instruction as outlined in Early Stage 1 and Stage 1. They will also need age-appropriate decodable texts to practise reading. These students must be given additional instruction, with intervention continuing until the extended phonics code has been mastered and skills are automatic.
  • Some students will achieve Stage 2 outcomes for Creating Written Texts during Year 3 and will need to be extended by accessing content at a higher stage.
  • In Stage 4, some students may not be able to access texts that are complex in their construction. These students must be given support to develop their skills through explicit teaching and consideration of the content in the Stage 3 Reading Comprehension outcome.

The importance of language in English

Students’ knowledge and understanding about language will grow and deepen as they engage with increasingly complex texts across a range of modes. Students continue to develop their understanding of how language use at word, sentence, paragraph and whole text-level, is determined by context, audience and purpose. Students’ knowledge of their first language will support this development.

The development of students’ vocabulary and background knowledge can be supported by their teachers engaging them in rich discussion and analysis of a range of texts, including those widely regarded as quality literature. This can support students’ comprehension and has the potential to expand their ideas and experience of both their own world and the world of others. As students deepen their knowledge of language, they can apply new understanding to purposefully communicate their ideas, with increasing confidence and efficacy. Through knowledge and understanding of language, students can appreciate, reflect on and enjoy texts that are widely regarded as quality literature.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Courses 7–10

The English K–10 Syllabus includes 2 courses for English 7–10:

  • English
  • English Life Skills

Focus of learning

In the study of English, students develop knowledge and skills to respond to and compose texts for a range of purposes. Students use strategies to read, view and listen to texts for understanding, challenge, interest and enjoyment.

What students learn

Students learn to analyse how meaning is created through the use and interpretation of increasingly complex language forms, features and structures. They examine, explain and evaluate how texts represent ideas and experiences and consider how texts can affirm or challenge values and attitudes. Students investigate and explain ways of valuing texts and the connections between texts.

Students learn to craft personal, creative and critical texts for a range of audiences by experimenting with and controlling language forms and features to shape meaning. They use processes of planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting to purposefully develop and refine their composition of texts.

Course requirements

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the English K–10 Syllabus.

Text requirements English 7–10

Engaging with texts is central to the study of English.

Life Skills

For English Life Skills:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more English 7–10 Life Skills outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the English 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • Engaging with texts is central to the study of English. For English Life Skills 7–10, the Text requirements can be used as guidelines to provide relevant and meaningful teaching and learning opportunities that draw from a wide range of texts.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Understanding and creating a wide range of texts is central to the study of English. In 3–6 the term texts refers to print and digital forms of communication that include linguistic, visual, audio, gestural and spatial meaning-making systems. Quality examples of literature should be presented in print and digital mediums, as well as in multimodal, visual and spoken modes, including picture books.

Many types of texts are easy to recognise by their subject matter, forms and structures. Persuasive, informative and imaginative texts include a range of genres for different social purposes.

Texts have evolved over time for the purpose of communicating effectively with a range of audiences. Sometimes several elements from different types of texts can be included in a single text, resulting in a hybrid text. Hybridity can encompass genre, modality and form.

Literature

Literature is defined as a body of work that has enduring personal, social, cultural or aesthetic value. It comprises a dynamic and evolving range of fiction and nonfiction texts from diverse contemporary, historical and cultural contexts. Literature is a way of sharing experiences about and beyond readers’ lives while also creating empathy and opportunities for enjoyment.

Literature should be readily available to students in the classroom and updated regularly.

Across each year of learning, teachers must give students daily opportunities:

  • To be read to: Teachers can support the development of reading for pleasure. By reading aloud and engaging students in discussions, teachers provide students with access to texts beyond their immediate means, introducing them to new ideas and vocabulary and encouraging them to explore different ways of thinking.

Where listening to texts read aloud is not accessible for students, they should be read to using their preferred communication form(s).

  • For wide and deep reading: Students should independently read and respond to a wide range of texts of varied genres and topics, with increasing complexity. They should also read and respond to texts of personal interest. Students should read aloud and silently for meaning, to acquire new ideas and vocabulary for communication, and for enjoyment.

Students who are not reading independently and have not mastered the initial and extended phonic code may need access to age-appropriate decodable texts to continue learning and consolidating decoding skills.

Where reading aloud is not accessible for students, they can share their reading using their preferred communication form(s) or engage in silent reading.

  • For wide writing: Students need to practise and experiment with creating persuasive, informative and imaginative texts in different forms. These can be created in English and in other learning areas, in both print and digital modes. Students should practise their writing under a variety of conditions with varied parameters of length and time. Writing refers to the creation of texts rather than the skill of handwriting. Students should be encouraged to create texts using their preferred communication form(s), including through the use of assistive technology as required. Reading supports wide writing, giving students the knowledge to:
      • select appropriate language suited to purpose
      • adapt and experiment with language
      • use textual elements from different genres and modes. 

Text selection

As teachers identify what their students need to learn at points in time, they select texts to facilitate that learning. Text selections should respond to the individual needs of students. Texts should be selected that either support or extend students’ reading. Selecting high-quality texts enables students to study features within and between texts. It can also enhance their knowledge, understanding and experience of others and of how texts represent the world. High-quality texts can support students to apply their language learning to new contexts for both reading and writing.

The selection of texts must include:

  • texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • Australian literature
  • literature from other countries.

Across a year of learning, the selection of texts must give students opportunities to engage with a variety of literature that includes strong examples of:

  • narrative
  • characterisation, including examples of stereotypical and archetypal characters
  • imagery, symbol and connotation
  • genre
  • theme
  • context and perspective
  • argument and authority.

Literature must include:

  • novels (may include quests, fantasy, science fiction, mystery novels)
  • plays
  • poetry
  • classic and contemporary literature that represents diverse experiences (may include literature by authors with diverse backgrounds and experiences, including authors with disability)
  • myths, legends, fables and fairytales
  • texts that provide information in different forms (may include everyday texts such as brochures, community publications, recipes, advertisements)
  • texts that include persuasive arguments presented in different forms
  • hybrid texts (an imaginative text such as a narrative will typically have language features such as the use of dialogue but may also contain visual features such as diagrams and subheadings more typically seen in informative texts)
  • texts chosen by students for personal interest and enjoyment.

Text complexity

Text complexity may vary in:

  • ideas or knowledge
  • structure
  • vocabulary
  • sentence complexity
  • levels of meaning or subtlety
  • modal elements.

Most texts combine aspects of simple and complex features. As learning progresses, students can sustain reading of more complex texts for longer periods of time.

Teachers should preview all texts that students study in class. This allows teachers to identify potential areas for targeted teaching.

Diversity of learners

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) should be provided with opportunities to share their experiences of reading or viewing texts in their home languages or dialects. This can assist them to make meaningful connections between their home languages or dialects and Standard Australian English. For students for whom Auslan is their first language, this should include a variety of signed texts, which may be live or recorded. Students whose first language or home language is Aboriginal English may be considered EAL/D learners.

These students bring a richness of linguistic capital and experiences which should be valued so that all students can be active agents in their engagement with texts.

It is important to provide the opportunity for students to respond to and create texts using their preferred communication techniques and systems. This may include assistive technology (AT) and augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems such as:

  • gesture
  • signing (reference to signing as an augmentative and alternative communication method typically refers to Key Word Sign)
  • real objects
  • photographs
  • pictographs
  • pictograms
  • texts with enlarged print
  • audio books
  • braille
  • speech-to-text and text-to-speech applications
  • digital technology.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Engaging with texts is central to the study of English. In Years 7–10, texts should be understood to mean any written, spoken/signed, nonverbal, visual, auditory or multimodal communication.

The forms, features and structures of texts evolve over time for the purpose of communicating effectively with a range of audiences. Sometimes a number of elements from different types of texts can be included in a single text, resulting in a hybrid text.

Students undertake essential content, and work towards course outcomes, by engaging meaningfully with a range of texts. Teachers select texts based on their understanding of what students need to learn at particular points in time. A well-chosen text enables students to study features within and between texts that can enhance their knowledge, understanding and experience of how texts represent the world. Texts should be selected that either support or extend students’ reading.

Text selection

As the focus of learning in each Stage, students are required to engage meaningfully with:

  • at least 2 works of extended prose (including at least one novel)
  • at least 2 collections of poetry
  • at least 2 films
  • at least 2 drama texts (including at least one Shakespeare play in Stage 5)
  • a range of types of texts inclusive of short prose, visual, spoken, multimodal and digital texts.

Across each stage, the selection of texts must give students experiences of:

  • a range of fiction and non-fiction texts that are widely regarded as quality literature
  • a range of texts by Australian authors
  • a range of texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors
  • a range of quality texts from around the world, including texts about intercultural and diverse experiences (might include literature by authors with diverse backgrounds and experiences, including authors with disability)
  • a range of cultural, social and gender perspectives, including from popular and youth cultures
  • texts chosen by students for personal interest and enjoyment.

Teachers should preview the texts that they select to use as a part of students’ learning. This allows teachers to identify potential areas for targeted teaching.

Text complexity

Text complexity may vary in:

  • ideas or knowledge
  • structure
  • vocabulary
  • sentence complexity
  • levels of meaning or subtlety
  • modal elements.

Most texts combine simple, predictable, moderately complex and highly complex features. The selection of texts should provide opportunities for students to engage with features of texts that provide appropriate levels of challenge.

Diversity of learners

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) should be provided with opportunities to share and extend their experiences of reading or viewing texts in their home languages or dialects. This can assist them to make meaningful connections between their home languages or dialects and Standard Australian English. For students for whom Auslan is their first language, this should include a variety of signed texts, which may be live or recorded. Students whose first language or home language is Aboriginal English may be considered EAL/D learners.

These students bring a richness of linguistic capital and experiences which should be valued so that all students can be active agents in their engagement with texts.

It is important to provide opportunities for students to respond to and compose texts using their preferred communication techniques and systems. This may include assistive technology (AT) and augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems such as:

  • gesture
  • signing (reference to signing as an augmentative and alternative communication method typically refers to Key Word Sign)
  • real objects
  • photographs
  • pictographs
  • pictograms
  • texts with enlarged print
  • audio books
  • braille
  • speech-to-text and text-to-speech applications
  • digital technology.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Understanding and creating a wide range of texts is central to the study of English. In K–2 the term texts refers to print, digital or spoken forms of communication and includes fiction and nonfiction works. Many types of texts are easy to recognise by their subject matter, forms and structures, such as imaginative, informative and persuasive texts. Texts have evolved over time for the purpose of communicating effectively with a range of audiences. Sometimes a number of elements from different types of texts can be included in a single text, resulting in a hybrid text. For example, an imaginative text such as a narrative will predictably have language features such as action verbs and descriptive noun groups, but may also contain visual features such as speech bubbles, diagrams and subheadings more typically seen in informative texts.

The act of creating texts involves:

  • selecting the language appropriate to purpose
  • adapting and experimenting with language
  • using textual elements from different styles, modes and text forms.

Literature

Literature is defined as a body of work that has enduring personal, social, cultural or aesthetic value. It comprises a dynamic and evolving range of fiction and nonfiction texts from diverse contemporary, historical and cultural contexts.

Literature should be readily available to students in the classroom and updated regularly.

Across a year of learning, teachers must give students daily opportunities:

  • To be read to: Being read to supports children in acquiring new vocabulary from a text, gives students access to texts beyond their immediate means and supports the development of reading as pleasure. Independent reading should not supplant being read to. Where reading aloud is not accessible for students, they should be read to using their preferred communication form(s).
  • To read decodable texts: Decodable texts support beginning readers to use decoding strategies and practise their developing reading skills. Provide decodable texts for beginning readers in Early Stage 1, and as needed for students in Stage 1 and beyond.
  • For wide reading: Once students can consistently use phonic knowledge to decode words, the use of decodable texts does not need to continue. At this point, students should be reading a wide range of texts of increasing complexity and varied topics.
  • For wide writing: Students need to practise and experiment with creating written texts in English and all other learning areas. Specific opportunities for writing may be found in texts being read, or in other experiences that can provide real contexts, audiences and purposes.

Text selection

As teachers identify what their students need to learn at particular points in time, they can select texts to facilitate the learning. Text selections should respond to the individual needs of students. Texts should be selected that either support or extend students’ reading. A well-chosen text enables students to practise, enhance and transfer knowledge and skills they already have and apply this learning to new contexts.

Across a year of learning, the selection of texts must give students opportunities to engage with a variety of texts, including:

  • texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • Australian literature
  • picture books
  • poetry and texts that feature wordplay and figurative language
  • classic and contemporary literature which include cultural and linguistic diversity
  • narrative texts that include examples of character (the term ‘narrative’ refers to an account of events or related experiences that can be real or imagined)
  • texts that provide information in different forms
  • texts that include persuasive arguments presented in different forms
  • plays
  • decodable texts
  • a range of digital texts (Stage 1).

Text complexity

Text complexity may vary in:

  • ideas or knowledge
  • structure
  • vocabulary
  • sentence complexity
  • levels of meaning or subtlety.

Most texts combine aspects of simple and complex features. As learning progresses, students can sustain reading of more complex texts for longer periods of time.

Teachers should preview all texts that students study in class. This allows teachers to identify potential areas for targeted teaching.

Diversity of learners

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) should be provided with opportunities to share their experiences of reading or viewing texts in their home languages or dialects. This can assist them to make meaningful connections between their home languages or dialects and Standard Australian English. For students for whom Auslan is their first language, this should include a variety of signed texts, which may be live or recorded. Students whose first language or home language is Aboriginal English may be considered EAL/D learners.

These students bring a richness of linguistic capital and experiences which should be valued so that all students can be active agents in their engagement with texts.

It is important to provide the opportunity for students to respond to and create texts using their preferred communication techniques and systems. This may include assistive technology and augmentative and alternative communication (ACC) systems, such as:

  • gesture
  • signing (reference to signing as an augmentative and alternative communication method typically refers to Key Word Sign)
  • real objects
  • photographs
  • pictographs
  • pictograms
  • texts with enlarged print
  • audio books
  • braille
  • speech-to-text and text-to-speech applications
  • digital technology.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is understanding and responding to literature important?

Students benefit from their teacher reading literature to them that is more complex in structure, language and visual elements than the texts they may read independently. The process of reading, listening, questioning, and responding to quality literature provides a foundation for students to engage in reflective and critical thinking. Reading quality literature provides opportunities to explicitly teach text structure, character, narrative, imagery and perspective.

Reading widely to students should be undertaken as frequently as possible, ideally daily. Reading a wide range of literature to students:

  • helps lay the foundation for them to become good readers and writers
  • supports the development of oral language, vocabulary and grammar knowledge
  • provides opportunities for teachers to model fluent reading
  • fosters a love for reading
  • stimulates imagination
  • supports them to appreciate their own cultural heritage as well as those of others
  • provides new perspectives on their lives and the lives of others.

Where reading aloud is not accessible for students, they should be read to using their preferred communication form(s).

Rich talk about literature

The teacher should provide opportunities for students to respond to literature by engaging them in rich talk about the texts that they read aloud. This can involve focusing on character descriptions, key events in a story or interesting, emotive or playful language. To extend students and provide opportunities for critical and creative thinking, rich talk can focus on increasingly complex and abstract vocabulary and ideas. When teachers ask powerful questions, students can learn to make critical connections to read-aloud texts and respond to such questions as, ‘Who is telling the story?’, ‘What do you think that person wants us to think?’ or ‘Why do you think the character is poor?’ When students practise asking critical questions about the text, they are developing thinking skills that can lead to powerful insights into how texts work, how readers can become more aware of their place in the reading process, and where they fit into the social world that surrounds them.

During rich talk, the teacher provides opportunities for students to use their oral vocabulary to:

  • retell story events
  • share key ideas in an information text
  • identify how words connect within a text to convey a particular message.

Capitalising on opportunities to select target words from the texts for explicit vocabulary instruction provides opportunities for students to make connections in their learning (see teaching advice for Vocabulary).

Facilitate rich talk through a literature or yarning circle. These can be held in a designated school space, or the concept can be applied in the classroom context.

When using rich talk, it is important to ensure all students can participate. Some students with disability use a variety of verbal or nonverbal communication techniques or systems. It is important that students are supported to participate in discussions about texts using their preferred communication form(s).

Reading to writing

Students’ thinking and understanding about texts deepens through discussion and writing. Students should be provided with opportunities to share their thinking and explore their ideas in a more formal way.

Literature provides a model for high-quality writing and as such can be used as a ‘mentor’ for both teachers and students. Using mentor texts, teachers identify and explore the creative, informative or persuasive language and text features their students need to know about. Students can then use similar features, like characters, setting or images, when creating their own texts.

In Early Stage 1, many writing activities will be modelled by the teacher through shared, interactive or joint construction sessions as a whole class. As students observe their teacher writing like a writer, this supports them to learn about the power, value and art of English for communication, knowledge and enjoyment.

Teaching considerations

Teachers should select literature that:

  • introduces new and unfamiliar contexts and experiences
  • represents different and interesting perspectives
  • is rich in language and visual features
  • merits multiple readings for the purposes of deep study
  • provides a variety of models of language, text structures and features
  • includes diverse characters while avoiding stereotypical representations of culture.

During and after a read-aloud teaching episode, the teacher should encourage students to respond to the text. This can occur in a range of ways. For example, the teacher may invite students to:

  • ask questions
  • share related experiences
  • identify key ideas
  • discuss meanings beyond the literal
  • recount and/or represent the plot through drawing (e.g. describe what happened at the start, in the middle and at the end)
  • describe character traits in a narrative
  • describe the action(s) of a subject (e.g. actions of a character in a narrative)
  • express how elements of the story make them feel
  • express their opinion(s) about characters, plot, subject and/or themes
  • jointly or individually write a response to the text.

The teacher can provide opportunities for students to respond to literature in creative ways. For example, teachers might engage students through:

  • musical play (e.g. by rhythmically and/or melodically reciting a text, or by producing sound effects or music to accompany a text)
  • physical play (e.g. by dancing, mimicking poses, or enacting frozen moments)
  • dramatic play (e.g. by miming or acting out a text)
  • puppetry (e.g. by retelling a narrative using finger puppets or paper masks)
  • visual craft (e.g. by creating pop-up or floor map versions of a text).

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Opportunities to share narratives from their home language(s) or dialect(s) with the class and to make connections with their existing knowledge and understanding of narrative and literature will support students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) to demonstrate their strengths and interest in literature. Students will also benefit from opportunities to use home language(s) or dialect(s) to generate ideas when responding to texts and when engaging in talk about texts.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Understanding and responding to literature.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and Responding level 1 and 2, Writing level 1 and Oral interaction level 4 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

content.value:
What is oral language and communication?

Oral language refers to joint processes of speaking and listening.

Speaking is the process of presenting meaning through the construction of spoken words. It involves appropriately enunciating speech sounds, using tone, pitch, stress and pace effectively. Listening is the process of attending to and constructing meaning from spoken texts. It involves distinguishing the sounds of words and being sensitive to tone, pitch, stress and pace.

Communication encompasses a system of expression and translation of spoken words, and using nonverbal communication modes such as gesture. Some students may need to develop skills in using augmentative and alternative forms of communication (AAC) to supplement or replace oral language. AACs can be unaided or aided. Unaided AACs include gestures, facial expressions and signs, such as Key Word Sign. Aided AACs include symbols, objects, pictures and voice output communication aids. The most appropriate AAC should be considered for each student. Some students may also use a combination of communication forms.

Oral language and context

Social conventions for language vary according to context. The way students listen, speak and respond to family and friends may differ from how they might carry on a conversation in more formalised settings, such as the classroom. Oral language and nonverbal forms of communication are used and interpreted differently across cultures, and a student’s cultural background and home language influences the way they communicate. Some students may communicate in ways that differ from expectations in the school context. Teacher awareness and understanding of this diversity can support students to understand and navigate the protocols and conventions for communicating in different contexts.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

For students with little or no exposure to Standard Australian English (SAE), it is important to identify where students are at in their development of proficiency in SAE. Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) can take up to 2 years to develop Basic Interpersonal Communication Skills in SAE. EAL/D learners may also go through a silent period in the early phases of learning SAE. A focus on receptive language and allowing students to communicate when they are comfortable will support their oral language development.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Speaking and Listening modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Oral language and communication.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Oral Interaction level 4 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

Students with complex communication needs

Students with complex communication needs may have different levels of receptive and expressive communication. Students who primarily communicate using nonverbal language need to be supported to develop communication skills using their preferred communication form(s). Some students’ preferred receptive communication form(s) may be different to their preferred expressive communication form(s).

Intentionality

Students with complex communication needs will be communicating at different levels of intentionality.

Communication is intentional if:

  • a student consciously directs a message towards another person
  • a student intentionally uses communicative behaviour(s) to send an explicit message to another person.

Students who communicate intentionally show an awareness that a communication partner’s attention must be gained for the message to be received. Intentional communicators assess a partner’s focus of attention and employ strategies to gain, shift or wait for their attention.

Intentional communicators may use non-symbolic and/or symbolic forms to communicate. Students at the symbolic level understand that the symbol(s) represent something else (a referent).

Functions

Students will communicate for a variety of purposes or functions. Students will have greater control over their environment if they are able to communicate using more established communication functions. Examples of communication functions include:

  • expressing needs and wants
  • transferring information
  • social relating
  • expressing feelings and states
  • internal dialogue.

Teaching strategies

Strategies that can be used to support students’ expressive communication include:

  • Active listening: involves the communication partner modelling appropriate body language, as well as validating and interpreting what the student is saying. This allows the student to feel heard and may increase their desire to communicate. It also develops the student’s understanding of the purpose of a communication partner.
  • Wait and signal: pausing and providing a prompt for the student to respond to. This can be used to develop students’ communication skills in response to questions or in social interactions, such as structured play. This supports latency time, which can vary for students with complex communication needs.
  • Contingent responding: involves back and forth conversations, where the communication partner responds to and builds on the student’s communication. This helps develop turn-taking in conversations and validates the role of the communication partner to the student.
  • Structured opportunities: creating situations that encourage and increase the student’s desire to communicate. This can include using high-value activities or topics of high interest to increase the intrinsic motivation and the desire to communicate.
  • Consistency: using repetitive or similar strategies across environments and communication partners. This allows the student to feel safe communicating in new environments or with new communication partners as language and message is consistent.

Further information about supporting students with complex communication needs can be found on the NESA website. It includes instructions and resources for identifying students’ needs, as well as strategies to support students.

Follow up

Early identification and suitable intervention(s) make a difference in students’ lives. Challenging behaviours may be an indication that the student is experiencing difficulties with speaking and listening. It is important to seek information from parents and caregivers about how the student uses their speaking and listening skills at home. Decisions about assessments by speech or hearing specialists should be considered in collaboration with parents and caregivers.

Additional opportunities for guided and independent practice may be required, either in the classroom or through specific interventions. Early intervention to support the development of speech and language skills is essential. Decisions about adjustments for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

What is vocabulary and why is it important?

Vocabulary can be categorised as receptive word knowledge (i.e. words that are understood when others use them) and productive word knowledge (i.e. words that are used orally or in written form).

Vocabulary can also be considered in terms of its breadth and depth. Breadth of vocabulary refers to the number of words an individual knows the meaning of. Depth of vocabulary means the words an individual can define (i.e. words they can provide attributes of and supply examples of other semantically related words) and use in a range of contexts.

Learning English vocabulary is one of the most crucial tasks for English learners as it is vital to reading success and to literacy development more generally.

Vocabulary contributes to young children’s phonological awareness and connects the word-level process of phonics and the broader cognitive process of comprehension, which in turn contributes to improvement in reading comprehension and writing.

Vocabulary plays a key role in the development of comprehension skills in all subject areas as students need to understand around 90 per cent of words to comprehend a text. Therefore, explicit teaching of carefully selected words is important for vocabulary acquisition, reading comprehension and creating written texts. Students in K–2 primarily learn vocabulary through oral language. Beyond this, vocabulary is largely learnt through reading and exploring texts. Students who communicate using nonverbal modes of communication should be provided with opportunities to learn new vocabulary using their preferred communication system. For example, using Key Word Sign, or through real objects, photographs or symbols.

Teaching vocabulary

A robust approach to teaching vocabulary should involve:

  • explicitly teaching selected words
  • explicitly teaching word-learning strategies
  • promoting word consciousness
  • providing rich and varied language experiences.

Explicitly teaching words

Explicitly teach students that a word is a group of letters that has meaning when spoken or written. Display the written word. Model this with individual word - for example, ‘This is the word fish. A fish is an animal that lives in fresh or salt water. It has gills to breathe through and it has scales on its body.’ Plan for words that will be the target of teaching (target vocabulary). These words can be selected from texts read to the students or concepts from Mathematics and other learning areas. It is not possible to teach all the new words that students will encounter throughout the year. Therefore, words targeted for explicit instruction need to be carefully selected. Beck, McKeown, and Kucan (2013) devised a 3-tiered framework to classify words as follows: Tier 1 words are basic-level words (e.g. dog, baby, happy, pretty). While we need to teach students how to read and write these words, they rarely require instruction at school in terms of what they mean and how to use them. Tier 2 words are of ‘high utility for mature language users and are found across a variety of domains’ (e.g. precede, stale, awful, snuggle). Tier 2 words add power and precision to written and spoken language but many Tier 2 words are most commonly found in written language. Tier 3 words are used rarely (low frequency) and only in highly specific situations (e.g. decibel, octave, atom).

The Three tiers of vocabulary posters: English K–6 are available as one downloadable document to support teachers’ and students’ understanding of vocabulary.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Vocabulary learning opportunities may include words in students’ home language. This can promote:

  • students making connections with their home language
  • all students to learn new words in a range of languages and/or dialects.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require supplementary teaching of Tier 1 words.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Reading/viewing, Writing, Speaking and Listening modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Vocabulary.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and Responding level 1, Writing level 1 and Oral Interaction level 4 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

The importance and development of creating written texts

Writing is an important tool for communicating and learning. It provides a mechanism for sharing information, telling stories, creating imagined worlds, and chronicling experiences and feelings. It can also be used as a powerful influencer.

Learning to write is a complex process that integrates knowledge and skills in text creation, print conventions, grammar, punctuation, vocabulary, spelling and handwriting. These competing actions involve the execution and coordination of motor, visual, executive functioning, memory, as well as knowledge and understanding of language and writing processes. If these actions necessitate too much attention for the writer, the cognitive system becomes overloaded and can impact the quality and quantity of the written product. Teachers should plan for these skills to be integrated and organised sequentially to support systematic and explicit teaching of writing, assessment and monitoring of student writing progress, all based on the students’ knowledge and skills.

Students may communicate written texts in alternative formats and through assistive technology, including:

  • text-to-speech devices
  • speech-to-text devices
  • keyboard or switch devices
  • AAC devices
  • communication boards
  • symbol-making software
  • word-prediction software.

Language, writing and reading

Developing a writing vocabulary requires a child to transfer words – which exist in the mind as non-verbalised thinking – into a set of marks on paper. Therefore, oral language, along with the ability to hear and record speech sounds and develop vocabulary, are important to writing development, which is in turn important for literacy development and success at school more generally.

Learning to write and learning to read should be treated as co-dependent processes. Mentor texts provide models for consolidating knowledge about different kinds of texts, sentence types, grammatical usage, vocabulary choice and punctuation. A focus on learning to write with correct grammar and punctuation also helps students in reading comprehension and fluency.

Teaching sentence-level grammar and punctuation

Explicitly teach the concept of a sentence. Explain that a sentence is a group of words that make a complete message.

Through explicit teaching, demonstrate a range of sentence structures, variability of sentence length and sentence beginnings to show how these can impact the effectiveness of the message being communicated.

Teaching word-level knowledge

Explicitly teach the function of nouns, verbs, pronouns, articles and adjectives and identify them in texts. When discussing word choices, encourage students to draw on both their personal vocabulary as well as words on display and in mentor texts.

If a student is not able to spell a word in the context of their writing, encourage them to have a go, drawing on their emerging phonic and spelling knowledge, but also by making printed words visible and easily accessible to the students where needed.

Teaching planning and revising

Ensure time for planning and discussion before students begin writing. Discuss what is going to be written. Model and think aloud aspects of the punctuation, sentence structure and ideas. Re-read the modelled version aloud and discuss the different aspects that are to be the focus of the lesson.

Students should have opportunities to practise what they are explicitly taught, discuss their writing, edit their writing after receiving feedback from the teacher and play with language in the form of words and sentences. Students should be given opportunities to apply their knowledge and skills in a widening variety of contexts as their writing develops. The aim is to have students achieve increasing control over and confidence in writing.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Identifying an English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) learner’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Creating written texts.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Writing level 1 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is handwriting and why is it important?

Handwriting is the formation, size, spacing, position and placement of alphabetic letters on a page. Developing a fluent and legible handwriting style is an essential skill for writing. It supports learning to read through enhancing letter recognition. Handwriting can significantly influence reading and writing development, which impacts student confidence in expressing their ideas.

Handwriting fluency includes being able to write legible letters from memory using:

  • knowledge of letter names, sounds and formation patterns
  • adequate hand and eye–hand skills, such as fine motor abilities.

Students can be supported to develop handwriting skills through a range of adaptive tools.

Teaching strategies

Teachers can support students to develop handwriting skills by:

  • clearly demonstrating letter formation for each letter as it is introduced in conjunction with teaching phonics and spelling
  • providing explicit teaching followed by short daily practice sessions. Short, sharp and frequent handwriting lessons are likely to be more effective than longer, less regular lessons
  • using a consistent mnemonic or auditory cue to describe the letter formation
  • providing multisensory methods for students to practise the formation – for example, using a finger to write in the air or on the carpet
  • encouraging students to immediately practise the letter formation pattern and encourage self-talk as the letter is practised
  • providing opportunities for students to consolidate taught letter formations – for example, by using small whiteboards where appropriate
  • providing opportunities for students to practise at tables and chairs and in workbooks to support them to develop the postural and motor skills needed for fluent writing
  • noticing and providing explicit feedback on accurate letter formation
  • encouraging students to think about the starting point, the direction of the lines and the strokes that make the letter
  • scaffolding the learning by allowing students to progress from observing a model, to copying and/or tracing and then writing from memory
  • encouraging students to evaluate their own handwriting after practising – for example, asking them to circle the letter that they believe is formed very well.

Handwriting fluency

Class activities can be planned to further promote handwriting fluency. Examples include:

  • using various writing materials, such as crayons and chalk, for students to practise focus letters
  • allowing students to ‘rub out’ writing on a whiteboard by tracing over the letters using the same formation pattern as used to write them.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Identifying an English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) learner’s proficiency in the Writing mode of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Handwriting.

What is phonological awareness?

Phonological awareness involves the identification and manipulation of parts of spoken language, including words, syllables, onsets and rimes, and the individual speech sounds in words (phonemes).

Image long description: A horizontal row of circles shows how spoken language can be broken down into parts. The circles are labelled: sentence; word; syllable; rime and onset; and phoneme. Another, parallel row of circles provides examples for each language part. The example sentence is: ‘A beautiful rainbow was in the sky’; the example word is ‘rainbow’; the example syllables are ‘rain’ and ‘bow’; the example onsets and rimes are ‘r-ain’ and ‘b-ow’; and the example phonemes are ‘r/ai/n’ and ‘b/ow’.

Phonemic awareness is a subset of phonological awareness that involves the specific skill of identifying and manipulating individual speech sounds within words (phonemes).

Phonemic awareness and phonological awareness are aural and oral skills that allow children to understand that speech is made up of words, and that words are made up of distinct sounds and sound patterns. Phonological and phonemic awareness are highly predictive of early reading acquisition.

These terms should not be confused with phonics. Strong phonemic awareness skills give students an advantage in learning phonics. These skills make it easier for students to understand the relationships between phonemes and the letters and letter patterns that typically represent speech sounds in written language (called graphemes).

Phonemes are not always easy to distinguish because we don’t articulate them separately. They are buried in a constant stream of speech, or are co-articulated. Some phonemes are easily confused, so students should not be left to identify speech sounds in words unassisted. Phonemic awareness should be explicitly taught if children are to benefit from phonics instruction.

Phonological awareness follows a progression of skills and phonological processes. This includes blending and segmenting, which are essential strategies for word reading (decoding) and spelling (encoding).

Teaching phonological awareness

Teaching phonemic awareness has a strong effect on word reading and writing skills when combined with teaching students about the graphemes.

The first language spoken by students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may not contain certain phonemes present in Standard Australian English (SAE). As such, some of these students may need additional support with unknown phonemes.

Students develop phonological awareness through carefully scaffolded activities such as:

  • rhyming
  • syllabification
  • onset and rime
  • phonemic skills.

The phonemic awareness skills of segmenting and blending phonemes are the most critical because they are essential component skills required for reading words (decoding) and spelling words (encoding).

Where necessary, students can also be encouraged to apply taught phonological skills when reading and writing high-frequency words, subject-specific words and more complex vocabulary that they encounter.

A broad range of strategies can be used to teach phonological awareness, taking into consideration students’ preferred communication form(s). For example, students may use physical actions, concrete materials, pictures or symbols in place of or as well as oral language to demonstrate blending and segmenting.

Elkonin boxes may be used by all students when segmenting or manipulating phonemes.

Example 1:

In Figure 2, students touch each box as they say each phoneme for the word provided orally, for example ‘fan’.

Example 2:

In Figure 3, phonemes are manipulated with counters representing phonemes.

content.value:
What is phonic knowledge?

Phonic knowledge refers to the relationship between speech sounds (phonemes) and their letter symbols (graphemes).

There are 44 unique phonemes in Standard Australian English (SAE). These phonemes are represented by the 26 letters of the alphabet, either individually or in combination.

The home language spoken by students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may not contain certain phonemes present in SAE. As such, some of these students may need additional support with unknown phonemes.

Understanding and using the English alphabetic code is essential for fluent and meaningful reading and writing in English.

Phonic knowledge is demonstrated when students can:

  • accurately decode words that they read, by blending phonemes
  • accurately encode (spell) words that they write, by segmenting phonemes.

Acronyms

AcronymMeaning
GPCsgrapheme–phoneme correspondences
CConsonant phoneme
VVowel phoneme

A phoneme is one sound which can be represented by one or more graphemes. For example, ch/i/p equals 3 phonemes and is an example of a CVC word.

Examples of words associated with acronyms

AcronymExamples
VCat, it, in, on, an, is, as, if, of, up
CVCpin, pan, sit, sun, hot, bed, shop, chip, that, wish, fish, pack, luck, thing
CCVCstop, spot, flat, plan, drip, trip, grub, clip, clash, bring, flash, crash, black
CVCCjump, send, bend, land, sand, pest, list, best
CCCVCstrip, strap, strum, scrap

Initial phonics code

The initial phonics code encompasses frequently occurring GPCs, including single-letter graphemes and consonant digraphs (e.g. sh, th, ch, ck, ng). It also includes frequently occurring split digraphs (e.g. a-e, o-e) and some of the vowel digraphs (e.g. oy, ay). Introducing common split digraphs and common vowel digraphs at this stage of learning will support students to read and write some high-frequency words comprising these graphemes.

See Suggested instructional sequence for Early Stage 1: Phonic knowledge.

Decodable texts

Decodable texts are designed to support students’ emerging decoding skills as they apply and consolidate taught GPCs. They:

  • are phonically controlled texts written for the beginning reader and contain specific GPCs
  • provide students with the opportunity to practise their developing decoding skills to read words and develop automaticity
  • build the number of GPC combinations in a systematic and gradual way.

A high lesson-to-text match will more likely result in immediate success for beginning readers. As students learn new letter sound relationships, they will progress to more complex decodable texts that allow them to practise new and previously learnt GPCs. The use of decodable texts should not be protracted. Once students have mastered all components of the extended code, they should access natural language texts.

Considerations for selecting decodable texts

When selecting decodable texts, consider texts that:

  • have a clear sequence of GPCs that closely matches the sequence of instruction
  • progressively incorporate a variety of words which use the explicitly taught GPCs
  • promote blending by having approximately 80 per cent of the text which can be independently decoded using taught GPCs
  • use frequent graphemic representations of the target GPCs
  • systematically introduce high-frequency words
  • contain connected text and have correct grammar and punctuation
  • include a story or information that carries meaning
  • have appropriately sized text which is well-spaced across the page.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
What is reading comprehension?

Comprehension is the understanding and interpretation of what is read both during and after reading. The responses students make following reading demonstrate that students have understood what is read. Reading comprehension involves 2 overarching skills that work together:

  • the ability to recognise or pronounce the words (decoding)
  • effective language comprehension, making sense of the words on the page.

Successful reading comes from developing knowledge and skills for both.

Language comprehension involves being able to understand the words, sentences and whole text. At a surface level, this has some alignment with how well a reader understands spoken and written language. At a deeper level, it requires more complex understanding of individual words in the sentences they form and the integration of these words and sentences across a text.

The importance of constructing a mental model for a text

To gain meaning, a reader needs to construct a representation, or mental model, for the text they’re reading. For example, the reader may see some vocabulary they already know in the text, they could create a picture in their mind about the text or they could connect to known concepts, such as recognising the structure in which the text is presented.

In Early Stage 1, students will most frequently develop their mental models of texts by drawing on their personal experiences, rather than from other influences. For example, if a student has been to a farm, they will know that certain animals live on a farm and will bring this knowledge to the text they are reading. If they have never been to a farm, they will find it difficult to construct a mental model of a farm to support their comprehension of the text.

Using background knowledge

Good readers make connections between what they are reading and what they already know. Reading comprehension and listening comprehension require active construction of inferences that are implied in the text. Inferences rely on background knowledge and can relate to knowledge of the words encountered in the text or knowledge of the particular type of text and other connections that the reader makes. Teachers can activate background knowledge that the students already have prior to reading and build background knowledge when students do not have the experiences or vocabulary to relate to the text.

Previewing activities are ways to connect students’ prior knowledge of a text with what they will read. In Early Stage 1 these activities will be scaffolded. The teacher could, for example:

  • support students to identify known features in the text, such as the punctuation or a character they recognise
  • ask students guiding questions prior to their reading - for example, ‘Do you think you know what this story will be about?’
  • engage students in discussion about their text predictions.

Making predictions requires the use of conditional language structures, including multiple verb structures and tenses. For example, 'I think this story will be about visiting someone in the country' may be particularly challenging for students learning English as and additional language or dialect (EAL/D). Support students by providing multiple oral models for a range of sentence and language structures and ensuring students have lots of opportunities to practice using these.

Activating word meaning

A reader needs to read the words and understand them to make meaning from a text. Some meanings are explained in the text and some meanings can be inferred from the context. It is necessary to pre-teach unfamiliar or challenging vocabulary prior to reading. Basic definitional meanings and degrees of meaning for words are both important. Teachers can use student friendly language when defining unfamiliar or challenging words.

In addition to explicit teaching of specific vocabulary, support students to:

  • look for vocabulary they know in the text as they read
  • consider the meaning of known and/or unknown vocabulary by exploring the context
  • work out the meaning of a word, by asking or seeking help
  • pause to clarify the meaning of unknown words.

Be aware that not all languages have written traditions, so some EAL/D learners may find it difficult to understand individual words in texts. Providing visuals or real-life objects for key words in a text will help EAL/D learners connect meaning.

Understanding and connecting sentences

In Early Stage 1 students will benefit from understanding that words such as and, because, but, for, if, or, and when are used to connect sentence parts (phrases and clauses). In addition to explicit teaching on sentence level grammar, support students to:

  • discuss the meaning of conjunctions presented in the text they are reading. For example, ‘Because means the reason why something happened, or to explain’
  • engage students in activities involving rearranging the position of words in a sentence and discuss how word order changes the meaning in a sentence. For example: Jake was late because he got a taxi. / Jake got a taxi because he was late.

Understanding whole text

Discussing the purpose of reading with students complements explicit teaching about text purposes. Students should understand that some texts:

  • are written to help them practise their reading
  • are written to entertain or inform
  • may have multiple purposes.

Monitoring comprehension

Comprehension monitoring occurs when readers reflect on their own reading and understanding of the text. Students must be able to monitor and use strategies when comprehension breaks down. Self-monitoring also provides a form of feedback. In Early Stage One, focus initially on comprehension of texts read to students and repeated reading of decodable texts while students develop the skills to read text with greater independence in order to monitor comprehension. Support students to monitor their own reading by:

  • ensuring they activate their background knowledge prior to reading. Be aware that texts often require cultural knowledge that some students may not have experienced. Support these students to build the field or context of the text prior to reading
  • alerting them to stop when they know they have lost meaning when reading
  • having them re-read and check if they make an error
  • modelling asking oneself questions while reading. For example:
  • ‘Did that make sense?’
  • ‘I wonder why she did that?’
  • ‘What do I already know about this?’
  • modelling making a statement to clarify meaning – for example, ‘I knew he did it!'
  • explicitly teaching how visual cues in multimodal texts can infer meaning. For example, images in light colours could infer happy emotions, as opposed to images with dark colours, possibly inferring something scary.

Recalling details

Engage students in activities to recall details of the text, such as:

  • identifying key characters, events or information
  • sequencing events
  • recounting the relevant ideas
  • using information or events from different parts of the text to form an opinion.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Texts require cultural knowledge, and some students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may not have experience with the cultural context of a text. In these instances, it is important to build a shared knowledge about the context and events of the text before reading.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Reading/viewing mode of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Reading comprehension.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and Responding levels 1 and 2 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

system.name: MS ES1 Teaching advice for Reading comprehension

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
What is reading fluency?

Reading fluency refers to the ability to read words in text accurately, effortlessly, at an appropriate rate, with phrasing and expression that reflect the meaning of the passage. It has been referred to as the bridge from phonics to comprehension, as it involves both reading the words in the text accurately and gaining meaning from the text in the way that the author(s) intended.

Fluency involves automaticity and prosody:

  • automaticity refers to accurate word recognition at an optimal rate
  • prosody refers to reading with expression using correct phrasing, intonation and attention to punctuation.

Foundational skills in print conventions, phonic knowledge, vocabulary and spelling are critical to developing automatic word reading and word knowledge. These skills support students to become fluent readers and to gain understanding of texts that they read. For Early Stage 1 students in the beginning stages of learning to read, the instructional focus is on the accuracy of reading skills, rather than the rate of reading. Early Stage 1 students commence with becoming automatic at identifying graphemes, then blending those graphemes to read words and phrases, moving on to reading decodable connected text. Once students can accurately and confidently read connected decodable text then a focus on rate and prosody is appropriate.

Frequent reading opportunities are needed to develop fluency. Providing daily opportunities for beginning readers to practise reading, combined with modelled reading by expert readers, is paramount when teaching fluency.

Automaticity

As students begin to rely less on decoding, they can increasingly recognise words automatically. This enables them to become fluent word readers. Automaticity:

  • is a critical aspect of reading fluency and comprehension
  • enables the reader to attend to meaning
  • is dependent on phonic knowledge (part-to-whole-word knowledge).

Repeated encounters with words can help decoding to the point of accurate and automatic recognition.

Students should be given immediate opportunities to apply the phonic knowledge they have learnt to accurately and automatically read words by practising their reading with decodable texts.

Prosody

Prosody is reading orally with appropriate phrasing and expression that reflects and enhances the meaning of the passage. Students will need frequent opportunities to hear prosodic reading and to practise their own reading.

Repeated, expressive reading of short phrases, text extracts and poems contribute to Early Stage 1 students being able to read in a conversational manner.

system.name: MS ES1 Teaching advice for Reading fluency

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
What is spelling?

Spelling is an essential word-formation process when creating written texts. Spelling proficiency in the first year of school is important for writing and reading development.

Many words in Standard Australian English (SAE) originate from other languages, including Aboriginal languages. In Early Stage 1, students begin to learn that SAE spelling involves combining knowledge of phonemes, conventional letter patterns and word meanings.

To spell simple words and support their emerging spelling skills, students combine knowledge of:

  • speech sounds (phonology)
  • letter patterns and generalisations (orthography)
  • meaningful word parts and how they can connect (morphology).

Phonological, orthographic and morphological components

An evidence-based instructional approach involves explicit teaching of the phonological, orthographic and morphological components of spelling. The instruction should be targeted and may include small-group structures.

Words should be taught by explaining the phonological, orthographic and morphological features as appropriate. When using words to teach spelling generalisations and strategies, students should be taught their meaning and how to read and spell them.

Words for teaching spelling should be carefully selected using words students have learnt to decode. Words should follow a common pattern or generalisation; these may be orthographic or morphological.

Some Aboriginal students may need support to further develop code-switching between Aboriginal English and SAE in relation to spelling. Teachers should:

  • be aware of the linguistic features of Aboriginal English and how these may influence spelling, such as fricatives – for example, them/dem, home/ome
  • be aware of culturally specific terms and words from Aboriginal languages, which should not be ‘corrected’ when used contextually – for example, Blak, brudda, tidda, gammon.

Instruction should be targeted at the needs of the students. The Suggested instructional sequence for Early Stage 1: Spelling aligns with content specific to Early Stage 1: Phonic knowledge and may be used to inform instructional planning. Any instructional sequence used should also be used with reference to evidence gathered from systematic spelling error analysis.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Identifying an English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) learner’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Spelling.

What is Expressing ideas and composing texts?

Students compose texts that express and represent their ideas, experiences, perspectives, knowledge and understanding gained from engagement with texts.

These skills and strategies are developed through exploring: the functional components of writing, representing and speaking; the stylistic elements that shape meaning in the creation of texts in a wide range of forms, media and modes, including written, aural, visual and multimodal texts; and the process of composition, including planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers should provide students with a broad range of opportunities to compose texts by designing learning experiences that include a range of modes, including multimodal responses.

How do I assess this focus area?

The outcomes for this focus area should be assessed in conjunction with outcomes from other focus areas. This assessment should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate.

Using the content, teachers can assess students’ development of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills required for expressing ideas and composing texts. Some students with disability may require adjustments when composing texts.

Students' progress can be observed when they are expressing ideas through the composition of texts.  Students should be provided with multiple opportunities to demonstrate their knowledge, understanding and skills in planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting on their work.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

All students can benefit from explicit modelling of the vocabulary and structures needed to compose a range of texts, and this is a particularly useful strategy for students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D). EAL/D learners may benefit from using their home language(s) and/or dialect(s) when planning written tasks and when reflecting on their work.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Expressing ideas and composing texts B.

Teachers can use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and Responding level 7, Writing level 7 and Oral interaction level 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
What is Understanding and responding to texts?

As the central focus of learning in English, students develop their knowledge and understanding of texts in order to compose responses in a range of modes and for a range of contexts, purposes and audiences.

Students learn to understand and respond to texts through exploring how textual forms and features, aesthetic qualities, voice, and structural components of texts, represent ideas and values. They develop an understanding of how texts from different historical, social and cultural contexts may challenge or reflect the values and perspectives of groups and individuals. They also build an understanding of how texts can be understood in relation to one another.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers should design learning experiences that require students to consider how forms and features of texts shape the representation of ideas and values, and connections and relationships, and how meaning is conveyed in the texts of others and in their own texts.

How do I assess this focus area?

The outcomes for this focus area should be assessed in conjunction with outcomes from other focus areas. This assessment should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate.

Using the content, teachers can assess students’ development of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills required for understanding and responding to texts. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access and respond to texts.

Students' progress can be observed when they are engaging with the ideas, perspectives and values in texts, and how these are communicated and understood. Students can demonstrate their understanding through written, spoken, visual and multimodal responses. Where the mode of response has been prescribed by the teacher, this should not preclude students from using their preferred communication form(s). Assessment of this focus area should consider the texts of others and students’ own texts.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Explicit teaching of vocabulary, cultural references and context will support all students to engage with and challenge the ideas, perspectives and values represented in texts. This strategy will be particularly useful for students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D). Modelling of language forms and features to express argument and authority, followed by opportunities to practise these skills, will support students to respond to and/or demonstrate their understanding of texts. Students may benefit from using their home language(s) and/or dialect(s) when generating ideas for written responses.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Understanding and responding to texts B.

Teachers can use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding level 7, Writing level 7 and Oral interaction level 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.
