value.name: english-2-3-reading-fluency.png
value.description: Factors that impact writing. More detail in text below.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
As students progress into Stage 1, writing contexts should cover both personal experience and content they are learning about in other areas of the curriculum. Across each of the Stage 1 learning areas, students have opportunities to practise and consolidate writing descriptions and explanations, and to build a wider vocabulary incorporating topic-specific words from other learning areas. They learn to write informative, persuasive and imaginative texts.

Written texts may be communicated by students in alternative formats and through assistive technologies, including:

  • text-to-speech devices
  • speech-to-text devices
  • keyboard or switch devices
  • augmentative and alternative communication devices
  • communication boards
  • symbol-making software
  • word-prediction software.

Teaching sentence-level grammar and punctuation

To support students with their sentence-level writing, a metalanguage needs to be established for describing how sentences and words work together to make meaning. Metalanguage enables teachers and students to engage in focused discussions about how language works in mentor texts and in their own written texts.

Students need to be taught explicitly how to identify and write different sentence structures. Teachers support students to understand the 4 types of sentences:

  • statements
  • questions
  • exclamations
  • commands.

Extracts from mentor texts can be used to check that students can distinguish a:

  • sentence
  • clause
  • phrase.

During explicit teaching sessions, and when students write, teachers:

  • model how to combine 2 simple sentences to form a compound sentence using coordinating conjunctions
  • model ways to expand sentences using prepositional phrases and/or noun groups
  • encourage students to experiment with different adverbs to modify the meaning of verbs or adjectives in their writing
  • demonstrate a range of sentence structures, variability of sentence length and sentence beginnings to show how these can influence the message being communicated
  • provide many opportunities for students to independently write their own sentences across a range of writing contexts
  • teach punctuation conventions (for example, quotation marks for dialogue), explain the use of punctuation in mentor texts and model the use of punctuation during modelled and shared/interactive writing lessons
  • provide many opportunities for students to practise using punctuation in independent writing activities.

Teaching word-level language

Students should be engaged in rich and purposeful discussions about how words can be carefully chosen in their writing to convey a nuanced and precise message.

When discussing word choices, they should be encouraged to draw on both subject-specific vocabulary as well as words on display and in mentor texts.

If a student is not able to spell a word in the context of their writing, they should be supported to have a go, drawing on their phonic and spelling knowledge, but also by making printed words visible and easily accessible to them where needed.

Also refer to the teaching advice on Vocabulary

Teaching planning and revising

To support the writing process:

  • explicitly teach students how to brainstorm and classify ideas for writing
  • provide suitable graphic organisers to assist with planning to write
  • model how to use graphic organisers when planning to write
  • use think-alouds when modelling the process of writing and during shared/interactive writing episodes
  • ensure learning intentions are visible and clearly articulated
  • provide immediate and corrective feedback as needed so that students know how they can improve their writing.
  • offer opportunities for students to collaboratively build their background knowledge in preparation for writing for a particular context, purpose and audience
  • provide ample time and opportunity for students to develop ideas for writing, and to structure and revise sentences and paragraphs so that they are cohesive
  • provide opportunities for students to decide on an authentic purpose for writing and to identify who the target audience will be
  • use metalanguage when discussing key features of a text to be written for a particular context
  • ensure a range of tools are available so that written texts can be enhanced through different modes and media.

Further support

Additional opportunities for guided and independent practice may be required, either within the classroom or through specific interventions. Early intervention to support the development of literacy skills is essential. Decisions about adjustments for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Some students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may have difficulty with sentence and text structure and writing processes when creating written texts. For example, punctuation and word order are used differently across languages. In some languages, punctuation does not exist. Not all languages have written traditions, so some EAL/D learners may require support to understand the links between spoken and written language.

Strategies that can support EAL/D learners to create written texts include:

  • explicitly teaching punctuation and grammar in context, so that students understand the feature and its purpose
  • explicitly teaching sentence structure and word order, rather than relying on self-correction, such as ‘does that sound right’?
  • providing frequent experiences of hearing English texts read aloud
  • using visuals or real-life objects to support the use of vocabulary in writing
  • using modelling and deconstruction of sentence and text features.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Creating written texts.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Writing level 3 and 4 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners within this focus area.

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Creating written texts

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Developing a fluent handwriting style enables the writer to focus on higher-order text-generation skills. A legible handwriting style is also important for the reader.

Students typically begin Stage 1 knowing how to form all lower-case and upper-case letters. Throughout Stage 1, they continue to refine their handwriting. Letter formations become:

  • increasingly faster
  • consistent in size, slope and spacing.

Teachers should closely monitor and provide immediate corrective feedback on:

  • writing posture
  • pencil grasp
  • letter formations.

Developing handwriting skills

Teachers support students to develop handwriting skills by providing explicit teaching followed by short daily practice sessions. Short, sharp and frequent handwriting lessons are likely to be more effective than longer, less regular lessons.

Continued practice of letter formation from memory, building on the basis from Early Stage 1, will assist students to develop an automatic, fluent handwriting style. Similar strategies to Early Stage 1 may assist at the beginning of Year 1 – for example, emphasising letter families with similar directional properties and encouraging accurate letter formation from memory.

Teachers can build on Early Stage 1 letter formation foundations by introducing concepts of:

  • letter placement on the line
  • spacing between words.

Spacing and line position

Students should be encouraged to leave a finger space (about 1.5 cm) between their words.

Visual cues for teaching handwriting can benefit students learning to produce letters. For example, paper may be used to guide the placement of letters (e.g. ‘dotted thirds’). Another example is shown below:

  • sky (top area)
  • grass (middle area)
  • soil (bottom area).

Students begin with lines that are widely spaced. As they develop control and fluency of the letter formations, the width between the lines is narrowed.

Students with low vision, or visual perception difficulties, may require additional support to develop handwriting skills. When teaching spacing, line position and letter formation, students may need to use enlarged lined paper, paper with thicker or bolder lines, or even tactile lined paper.

Letters

To teach consistent size teachers ensure that:

  • tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t) are tall
  • tail letters (g, j, p, q, y) have a long enough tail
  • short letters (a, c, e, i, m, n, o, r, s, u, v, w, x, z) are short and positioned correctly on the line.

Digital technology

Students in Stage 1 also expand and apply their knowledge of digital technology when creating texts.

For example, students:

  • know how to create a table or simple diagram
  • develop increasing response times when typing familiar words
  • can include punctuation or other symbols when creating digital texts.

Some students may be unable to produce handwriting, even with the use of adaptive tools and supports. These students will need to engage with digital technology and be provided with explicit instruction to develop skills to use digital technology independently to create written texts.

Computer keyboarding skills

It is important to support students when they are first developing computer keyboarding skills. Letters on the keyboard get covered up when the student types. Place stickers or pieces of tape with letters on their home row fingers. This allows the student to see which finger controls each letter.

Assistive technology

Handwriting and digital technology skills may be supported using appropriate assistive technology. For example:

  • adaptive writing tools and paper, such as dark felt-tip markers, adaptive grips and holders on writing tools, and dark line or braille paper
  • speech output and screen magnification on digital devices
  • eye gaze technology to produce written text
  • adaptive switches to operate devices to produce written text
  • augmentative and alternative communication to produce written text.

Eye gaze

Students using eye gaze to produce written text digitally should be provided with opportunities to develop early vision skills. These skills include:

  • looking at images – for example, detection and fixation
  • visual attention – for example, sustained fixation
  • tracking – for example, fixation and smooth pursuit movements
  • recognition – for example, perception and memory skills
  • inspecting – for example, shifting gaze and saccadic movements
  • searching – for example, discrimination and comparison skills.

Further support

Additional opportunities for guided and independent practice may be required, in the classroom or through specific interventions. Early intervention to support the development of literacy skills is essential. Decisions about adjustments for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Some students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may lack familiarity with technology and/or alphabetic knowledge in English and may benefit from explicit modelling and support with writing and typing skills.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Writing mode of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Handwriting.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
In Stage 1, oral language skills continue to play a key role in:

  • sharing and expressing ideas
  • clarifying and refining thoughts
  • providing a scaffold for students to comprehend more abstract concepts across the curriculum.

Some students may need to develop skills in using augmentative and alternative forms of communication (AAC) to supplement or replace oral language. AACs can be unaided or aided. Unaided AACs include gestures, facial expressions and signs, such as Key Word Sign. Aided AACs include symbols, objects, pictures, and voice output communication aids. The most appropriate AAC should be considered for each student. Some students may also use a combination of communication forms.

Social and learning interactions often require knowledge and understanding of how complicated language conventions work. These conventions can change depending on the situation or who we are communicating with.

Early identification and suitable intervention(s) make a difference in students’ lives. Challenging behaviours may be an indication that the student is experiencing difficulties with speaking and listening. It is important to seek information from parents and caregivers about how the student uses their speaking and listening skills at home.

Decisions about assessments by speech or hearing specialists should be considered in collaboration with parents and caregivers.

Additional opportunities for guided and independent practice may be required, in the classroom or through specific interventions. Early intervention to support the development of speech and language skills is essential. Decisions about adjustments for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

For students with little or no exposure to Standard Australian English (SAE), it is important to identify where they are at in their development of proficiency in SAE. Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) can take up to 2 years to develop Basic Interpersonal Communication Skills in SAE. EAL/D learners may also go through a silent period in the early phases of learning SAE. A focus on receptive language and allowing students to communicate when they are comfortable will support their oral language development.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Speaking and Listening modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Oral language and communication.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Oral Interaction level 5 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Understanding and using the Standard Australian English (SAE) alphabetic code is essential for fluent and meaningful reading and writing in English.

Phonics refers to the relationship between speech sounds (phonemes) and their letter symbols (graphemes).

There are 44 unique phonemes in SAE. These phonemes are represented by the 26 letters of the alphabet, either individually or in combination.

The home language(s) or dialect(s) spoken by students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may not contain certain phonemes present in SAE. As such, some of these students may need additional support with unknown phonemes. 

Phonic knowledge is demonstrated when students can:

  • accurately decode words that they read by blending phonemes
  • accurately encode (spell) words they write by segmenting phonemes.

Acronyms used in the syllabus for phonic knowledge

AcronymMeaning
GPCsgrapheme–phoneme correspondences
Cconsonant phoneme
Vvowel phoneme

In the following examples, the letters CCVCC or CCCVC refer to words with 5 phonemes. A phoneme is one sound. Some phonemes can be represented with more than one grapheme. For example, the digraphs ch, sh, th represent one sound. Splash has 5 phonemes and is an example of a CCCVC word, / s / p / l / a / sh / = splash. Scrunch is a CCCVCC word and has 6 phonemes as the digraph ch represents one phoneme, / s / c / r / u / n / ch /.

AcronymExamples
CCVCCstamp, stomp, stand, twist, crisp, frost, plant, trunk, drink, spend, blast, drift
CCCVCstrip, strap, strum, scrap, split, splat, splash, scream, screen, strain
CCCVCCscrunch, script, splint, sprint, strand

Initial and extended phonics code

In Stage 1, explicit and systematic phonics instruction is essential. Students consolidate knowledge of the initial phonics code when decoding (reading) and encoding (spelling) single-syllable words and multisyllabic words.

The initial phonics code includes frequently occurring single-letter graphemes and consonant digraphs (e.g. sh, th, ch, ck, ng). This syllabus expands this to include split digraphs, sometimes also referred to as ‘silent final e’ (e.g. a-e, o-e) and some commonly occurring and consistent vowel digraphs (e.g. oy, ay).

Students also master the extended phonics code and apply this to a range of reading contexts. This encompasses the broader range of graphemes for each corresponding phoneme. An example of the extended phonics code includes knowing the range of graphemes used to represent r-controlled vowels (e.g. ur in words like ‘hurt’, ir in words like ‘bird’ and er in words like ‘her’).

Teachers may use the suggested instructional sequence to inform their own instructional planning:

  • Aim to explicitly teach 2 to 4 GPCs per week. For some students, this rate may need to be slower to allow sufficient opportunity for consolidation. Other students may be able to advance more quickly. In Stage 1, when students have mastered the initial code, begin systematically teaching 2 to 3 graphemes for each phoneme at a time. To avoid cognitive overload, begin with the most common letter combinations. As students become familiar with those graphemes, expand the teaching to include other graphemes for each phoneme. There are many graphemes to represent the phoneme /or/, for example. Teach ‘or’, ‘aw’, ‘au’ (as in for, saw, sauce) before ‘ore’ and ‘our’ (as in more, your). Every spelling of /or/ does not have to be taught in Year 1; ‘ough’ and ‘augh’ (thought and taught) will be introduced later.
  • Introduce graphemes cumulatively and review these multiple times across the year, each time using new vocabulary
  • When teaching decoding and encoding skills, begin using one-syllable words and gradually progress to multisyllabic words.

See the Suggested instructional sequence for Stage 1: Phonic knowledge.

Decodable texts

Decodable texts are designed to support students’ emerging decoding skills as they apply and consolidate taught GPCs. They:

  • are phonically controlled texts written for the beginning reader that contain specific GPCs
  • provide students with the opportunity to practise their developing decoding skills to read words in order to develop automaticity
  • build the number of GPC combination in a systematic and gradual way.

A high lesson-to-text match will more likely result in immediate success for beginning readers. As students learn new letter–sound relationships, they will progress to more complex decodable texts that allow them to practise new and previously learnt GPCs. The use of decodable texts should not be protracted. Once students have mastered all components of the extended code, they should access natural language texts.

Considerations for selecting decodable texts

When selecting decodable texts, consider texts that:

  • have a clear sequence of grapheme–phoneme correspondence (GPC) that closely matches the sequence of instruction
  • progressively incorporate a variety of words which use the explicitly taught GPC
  • promote blending by having approximately 80 per cent of the text which can be independently decoded using taught GPC
  • use frequent graphemic representations of the target GPC
  • systematically introduce high-frequency words
  • contain connected text and have correct grammar and punctuation
  • include a story or information that carries meaning
  • have appropriately sized text which is well-spaced across the page.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
In Stage 1, students typically master the extended phonics code, while their decoding skills gradually become more automatic. At this point, the link between language comprehension and reading comprehension tightens. Students will encounter texts of increasing complexity and length over time and as appropriate to their individual progress and needs. The skills and strategies students will need to support their comprehension of independently read texts will continue to develop as they frequently practise reading and engage in deep conversations about texts, and with explicit teaching of text structures and language features.

It is important for teachers to frequently monitor their students’ comprehension when they are reading. While students may be ‘reading’ the words on a page, written language can be complex and difficult for many to grasp. Deep understanding of language in texts being read by students may also prove challenging and may need to be a focus for explicit teaching.

The importance of constructing a mental model for a text

When learning to read, students use their personal experience, prior knowledge of words, text structures and other concepts to create a mental model for a text. However, as students experience a broader range of texts in Stage 1, they will need to extract new understandings (new words, concepts and perspectives), from information they read in texts. These may either challenge or enhance their existing knowledge.

For example, if a student reads a text about a party and the word ‘piñata’ is presented, they may know about parties but may be confused about the meaning of ‘piñata’ and its association with parties.

While students are reading, support them to affirm and/or adjust their mental model of the text as new information is presented.

Using background knowledge

Familiarising themselves with the texts their students are reading allows teachers to identify potential breakdown areas in comprehension. For example, metaphors, idioms, and other literary devices are based on background knowledge. Language features such as these will need to be explicitly taught, particularly for students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D).

One such example is ‘It’s raining cats and dogs’. Such colloquial language is often used in everyday spoken language or when a writer is portraying informality. Teachers should not assume that students will know the meaning. It may be at odds with their existing understanding of rain and cats and dogs.

Students experiencing difficulties with comprehension may benefit from explicitly building the field of background knowledge before reading a text.

Additionally, teachers can draw upon awareness of students’ backgrounds, experiences and interests.

Developing positive relationships promotes open communication that can encourage students to seek assistance when required. Teachers can also use their knowledge of individual students and their preferences to select texts that students are more likely to relate to and engage with, including texts in students’ home language, or texts by or about a range of cultures.

Making inferences

Inferences are conclusions made by a reader based on:

  • evidence presented in the text
  • their prior knowledge and experience.

Inferences are necessary for readers to form their mental model for a text. For this reason, not all inferences will be used in the same way by readers.

While inferences are supported by the text, they also go beyond what is explicitly stated. Not all inferences are necessary for adequate comprehension and teachers need to support students to determine the importance of information for meaning-making when reading.

The following discussion scaffolds can be used for this purpose during small group and guided reading sessions or during whole-class interactions.

  • Who is the pronoun referring to in this sentence?
  • Am I supposed to know where Smith St is?
  • Is that important? I think that is important because…
  • I will need to underline – that will be important to remember…
  • This word is important because…
  • The layout of this text helps me work out what is important.
  • I must remember this when I retell, the order in which things happen is important.
  • I can summarise this by saying…
  • That’s important. I’ll need to write that down.

Activating word meaning

Previewing a text for known vocabulary and making connections for students, continues to be a sound strategy in Stage 1. So, too, does the explicit teaching of new words read in texts.

It is also important to consider that some meanings of vocabulary are explained and obvious in the text, but others may be implied.

For example, the word run in a sentence without an accompanying picture of a bus might say, ‘He made a run for it, but he didn’t make it.’ For some students, the notion of a run could be confusing without discussion. ‘Why did he run?’ and ‘What happened to him?’ may be questions that arise.

This highlights the importance of exploring words within and beyond the textual context in which they are encountered.

When students read, teachers:

  • encourage them to identify known vocabulary in texts
  • highlight taught morphemes and explain that they help to clarify the meaning of unknown words
  • scaffold students’ use of reference sources, such as dictionaries including bilingual dictionaries, to seek clarification for unknown words
  • discuss how vocabulary signals humorous wordplay in texts.

Understanding and connecting sentences

Connectives join 2 separate ideas in 2 sentences or paragraphs. Conjunctions join 2 ideas in the same sentence. Readers benefit from understanding the function of connectives in sentences and experiencing activities that highlight the different relationships that the 2 signal.

During explicit teaching sessions, and when students are reading, teachers support them to:

  • understand that coordinating conjunctions, (such as and, so, but, yet, or) are used to join 2 parts of a sentence that are grammatically equal - for example, ‘Jan and Pete went home’
  • understand that subordinating conjunctions (such as because, since, as, although, though, while, and whereas) link independent and dependent clauses and can express a cause-and-effect relationship - for example, ‘Jan went to bed because she was sick’
  • identify coordinating and subordinating conjunctions in complex sentences in texts they read or share
  • recognise that the important idea for the reader is influenced by position of a type of clause in a complex sentence
  • know that pronouns usually relate to other words preceding them in a text and that they are a type of cohesive device that can be used to bind sentences - for example, ‘Archie skipped all the way home, he was so happy’
  • know that pronouns are linked to nouns and need to be consistent within and across sentences and/or paragraphs for meaning
  • identify the words across sentences and/or paragraphs that infer meaning in texts they read or share.

Understanding whole text

Determining the features and structure of texts enhances comprehension. With explicit teaching, students learn that fiction and non-fiction texts are written for varied purposes and for a range of possible audiences. They understand that texts come in different forms with varying features that contribute to overall comprehension of the text. When students read, teachers can support them to:

  • use multiple sources of information to gain understanding of a text; for example, identifying characters, setting, plot, or a table of contents and graphs in a non-fiction text
  • identify and discuss the structure of a text prior to their independent reading
  • identify features and purposes for authentic texts such as brochures, letters and/or posters
  • identify and use navigation pathways appropriate for different types of texts
  • discuss their overall opinion of a text once they have coordinated information from its different parts.

Monitoring comprehension

Monitoring comprehension is a skill that students need to develop for effective comprehension. To gain meaning a reader will need to compare what they are reading with what they already know. They may need to adjust their existing knowledge in the light of new information being gained as they read. This comparison may result in conflict with the reader’s prior knowledge, which they will need to resolve. As this is a cognitive process, the reader will stop, think, and consider what to do to fix their reading problem.

When students read, teachers can support them to:

  • develop the field or context of the text prior to reading, particularly where students do not have experience with the cultural context of a text
  • monitor their own reading by registering a break in their comprehension
  • identify when their meaning is not complete and/or contradicts with their prior understanding
  • repeat words, phrases, or sentences to check, confirm or modify their reading
  • re-read a passage to enhance phrasing and clarify precise meaning
  • ask a clarifying question when more background knowledge is needed to make an inference
  • make text-to-self, text-to-text and text-to-world connections
  • predict and confirm their understanding through their knowledge of text structure, type, author, and forms
  • use their mental model to confirm their predictions and evoke personal reactions, such as ‘I didn’t think that before’
  • draw upon a range of visual and auditory features in multimodal texts to support their understanding
  • recall details in texts, such as key events and/or information
  • sequence and explain events and information in the text to confirm meaning
  • use written, visual or oral summaries to recount the relevant ideas from the text
  • enhance their understanding by interpreting patterns in the text
  • enhance their learning across key learning areas.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Texts require cultural knowledge and some students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may not have experience with the cultural context of a text. In these instances, it is important to build a shared knowledge about the context and events of the text prior to reading.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Reading/viewing mode of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Reading comprehension.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and Responding level 3 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Students in Stage 1 are consolidating knowledge of the initial phonics code and are mastering the extended phonics code. This learning is supplemented and enhanced by reading appropriately aligned, decodable texts aloud. Teacher monitoring of students’ phonic knowledge and their reading aloud is critical to determining when to progress students to a broader and more complex range of texts for independent reading.

Reading fluency requires well-established phonic knowledge and whole-word recognition. Immediate and accurate recognition of words allows the reader to concentrate on meaning rather than decoding. It’s a key factor in supporting young children to transition from beginner to fluent readers.

Fluent readers read a passage aloud for the first time with an easy speech rhythm and with few errors or self‑corrections. They change in their volume and pitch, and adopt grammatically appropriate pauses, with attention to punctuation that supports both reader and listener to access the author’s intended meaning for the text.

Teachers can support students in Stage 1 to:

  • know that reading accurately, effortlessly and with meaningful expression is the goal
  • vary their reading pace, adjust phrasing, intonation and volume, and to take note of punctuation
  • self-correct when fluency is interrupted
  • make few mistakes when reading aloud.

Considerations for teaching reading fluency

Oral reading

Oral reading occurs when printed text is read aloud. Engaging students in oral reading can promote reading confidence and enjoyment, and improved reading fluency.

Wide reading

Once children can read simple and/or more complex texts on their own, either for pleasure or for learning, their exposure to words grows rapidly. Ultimately, it is children’s own extensive, varied and rich experience in reading that will play the most important role in their transition from novice to expert readers.

Teachers can support their students to read a range of texts by making books and other texts readily available in the classroom. While independent reading is important, it should not supplant other reading instruction. Class time should be used for explicit instruction, frequent guided practice and scaffolded independent reading.

Monitoring and intervention

For some students, fluency may develop simply from practising their reading. Others who need to practise more often do not because it is difficult and labour-intensive. Students whose fluency does not develop easily may require significant additional support. If a student is lacking progress in oral reading fluency, early intervention is essential. Fluency is a component of reading that is difficult for older students to improve on. Early intervention is more efficient and effective than later attempts.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students in the early phases of English language learning may go through a silent period and so a focus on receptive language may be advisable. Some students may already have experience reading in their home language(s) and/or dialect(s) and will be able to draw on these skills to scaffold their reading progress.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Learning to spell is important for expanding vocabulary skills. It can enhance meaning-making when reading and writing. A student who is proficient at spelling is better equipped to focus on other important aspects of writing.

In Stage 1, students know that spelling is an important visible word-level language element of text creation. They understand that Standard Australian English (SAE) spelling involves awareness of:

  • speech sounds (phonology)
  • common letter patterns and rules (orthography)
  • how word parts signal meaning and grammar
  • how many words derive from different languages (morphology and etymology).

By the end of Stage 1, students can apply a combination of these strategies when spelling words across a range of topics and subject areas. They articulate a range of spelling strategies, including some generalisations for using suffixes.

Students demonstrate automaticity when spelling taught high-frequency words in a range of writing contexts. They can efficiently combine an awareness of speech sounds with knowledge of taught letter patterns and word-meanings when spelling.

Students also apply knowledge of taught spelling conventions when decoding words that are less familiar to them and when they revise and edit spelling errors in their own writing.

Teaching of spelling and vocabulary (including exploring word structures and how spelling can alter meaning) should be closely linked.

Instruction should be targeted to the needs of the students. The Suggested instructional sequence for Stage 1: Spelling aligns with content specific to Stage 1: Phonic knowledge and may be used to inform instructional planning. Any instructional sequence used should also be used with reference to evidence gathered from systematic spelling error analysis.

Phonological, orthographic and morphological components

An evidence-based instructional approach involves explicit teaching of the phonological, orthographic and morphological components of spelling. Ideally the instruction is targeted and in small-groups. Spontaneous revision of taught concepts, as opportunities arise, should also be embedded.

Phonological strategies

These may include:

  • syllabification
  • phoneme segmenting.

Students should be able to segment and blend all phonemes in one-syllable words before applying this strategy to multisyllabic words. They should be encouraged to orally segment words prior to writing them.

Orthographic strategies

These may include:

  • identifying the positional constraints of some graphemes. For example, knowing that words do not typically end with the grapheme oi but they can end with oy; and that i and u do not often end English words
  • identifying plausible letter sequences (the trigraph igh is plausible but ihg is not)
  • explaining how to use a dictionary and other spell-checking resources to check the spelling of an unfamiliar word
  • teaching contractions by explaining that words can be shortened by combining 2 words using an apostrophe to replace letter(s). For example, is + not = isn’t and I + will = I’ll. Explain to students that contractions can be used in less formal contexts
  • teaching word-specific orthographic knowledge using words that have infrequently occurring graphemes.

Morphological strategies

These may include:

  • identifying the meaning and function of the smallest meaningful units within a word (morphemes)
  • teaching students the rules associated with how to combine morphemes to produce a word.

Combining the study of morphemes with exposure to the origin of those morphemes (etymology) can be helpful to some students.

Etymology

Many words in SAE originate from other languages, including Aboriginal languages. In Stage 1, there is scope to discuss the etymology of words, especially words with uncommon grapheme–phoneme correspondences (GPCs).

For example, the word holiday can be discussed with students.

  • The word was first used in England hundreds of years ago and was written as haliday.
  • The letter i in the second syllable and that the original meaning was ‘holy day’.
  • Over time, the pronunciation, spelling and meaning of the word has evolved.

There is also scope to discuss how the names of many people, places and foods may derive from languages other than English – for example, how pizza and pasta are Standard Italian words.

Students should have opportunities to explore words that are borrowed from Aboriginal language(s) and/or dialect(s) – for example, gugubarra from Wiradjuri (central western NSW) represented in English as kookaburra, or placenames derived from the Aboriginal language(s) in the local area.

Refer to the Suggested instructional sequence for Stage 1: Spelling. The sequence aligns with content specific to Phonic knowledge and may be used to inform instructional planning. Irrespective of the instructional sequence that is used, ensure instruction is targeted to the needs of students. The instructional sequence should be used with reference to evidence gathered from assessment data, and this should include systematic spelling error analysis.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Where appropriate, teachers should take the opportunity to make connections with students’ cultural backgrounds and the home language(s) or dialect(s) of students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D). Some EAL/D learners may benefit from explicit teaching of letter-sound correspondence in SAE.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Spelling.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Vocabulary can be categorised as receptive word knowledge (i.e. words that are understood when others use them) and productive word knowledge (i.e. words that are used orally or in written form).

Vocabulary can also be considered in terms of its breadth and depth. Breadth of vocabulary refers to the number of words that an individual knows the meaning of. Depth of vocabulary means the words that an individual can define (i.e. words for which they can provide attributes and supply examples of other semantically related words) and use in a range of contexts.

A robust approach to teaching vocabulary should involve:

  • explicitly teaching individual words
  • explicitly teaching word-learning strategies
  • promoting word consciousness
  • providing rich and varied language experiences.

In Stage 1, students need to:

  • be explicitly taught new vocabulary
  • encounter unfamiliar words in meaningful contexts
  • have meanings of unfamiliar words explained
  • continue to apply newly acquired words.

Students should be provided with opportunities to:

  • use precise, descriptive and subject-specific words in their oral interactions and writing
  • make intentional oral and written word choices to elaborate on ideas or enhance meaning
  • use word-learning strategies introduced in class, with growing independence
  • use newly learnt words in specific and appropriate ways, for example, symmetry.

The Three tiers of vocabulary posters: English K–6 are available as one downloadable document to support teachers’ and students’ understanding of vocabulary.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require supplementary teaching of Tier 1 and Tier 2 words as well as support to distinguish the sounds in Standard Australian English (SAE). Engagement with students’ home language(s) or dialect(s) when discussing the meaning of new words may enrich the learning experience and allow students to connect their existing knowledge and skills about vocabulary.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Reading/viewing, Writing, Speaking and Listening modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Vocabulary.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and Responding level 3 and 4, Writing level 3 and 4, Oral Interaction level 5 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
What is oral language and communication?

Oral language refers to speaking (expressive language skills) and listening (receptive language skills) and is inherently social (Gee 2011).

Oral language develops knowledge of how language is used in context. Varied opportunities for oral language use in a range of contexts allows students to observe, understand and practise different language experiences for a range of purposes and audiences.

Communication encompasses a system of both reception and expression, as well as translation of spoken words and use of nonverbal communication modes such as gesture. Some students may need to develop skills in using augmentative and alternative forms of communication (AAC) to supplement or replace oral language. AACs can be unaided or aided. Unaided AACs include gestures, facial expressions and signs, such as Key Word Sign. Aided AACs include symbols, objects, pictures and voice output communication aids. The most appropriate AAC should be considered for each student. Some students may also use a combination of communication forms.

Oral language and communication should be embedded in learning experiences across a wide range of subject areas. They are supported by the environment, opportunities and interactions of language learning (Gross 2017).

Why is it important?

Oral language supports vocabulary learning and builds background knowledge. Background knowledge supports reading comprehension. Poor reading comprehension may indicate a need to further develop language comprehension. Furthermore, a student’s reading comprehension can often be constrained by their listening comprehension (Biemiller 2003). Therefore, teachers should support students to establish robust listening comprehension skills. Oral language is used when planning and creating written texts to support ideation, vocabulary and grammar. Receptive and expressive oral language skills have been found to relate directly to written text creation (Kim and Scatschneider 2017).

The oral language that students engage with becomes increasingly complex in Stages 2 and 3. Some vocabulary they encounter may be less familiar and sentences may be longer and harder to process semantically and syntactically. Students are also expected to make connections and inferences across longer stretches of language. Bridging the gap between a student’s everyday oral language and academic language is critical. This is particularly important for students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) as many EAL/D learners develop their oral language skills faster than their academic language skills (Cummins 2008).

Considerations for teaching

The most important initial step in developing a student’s oral language and communication is to understand students’ skills at the start of Stage 2, so that teaching begins at the point(s) of need. The content groups, Interacting, Listening for understanding and Presenting, will provide guidance for this.

Oral language and communication can be addressed in parallel with other focus areas. For example, when addressing:

  • vocabulary, students learn and use new words through dialogic communications facilitated by the teacher. This can ensure students are exposed to and use language for a range of purposes and audiences, which will help them to identify how language changes in different contexts
  • reading fluency, students apply taught skills such as intonation and stress during oral reading and when presenting
  • creating written texts, students participate in focused discussions when planning their written texts, or when incorporating multimodal elements into a prepared spoken presentation
  • understanding and responding to literature, students discuss textual structures, features and how literature engages them.

It is important students understand the difference between talk as a process, e.g. a discussion in a group setting to develop comprehension and talk as production e.g. speeches, and how oral language differs in these contexts.

Students with complex communication needs

Students with complex communication needs may have different levels of receptive and expressive communication. Students who primarily communicate using nonverbal language need to be supported to develop communication skills using their preferred communication form(s). Some students’ preferred receptive communication form(s) may be different to their preferred expressive communication form(s). The syllabus has included Complementary content to assist teachers to support students who use alternative communication forms. For more information refer to the NESA website.

Tone, pitch and volume can be hard to distinguish for d/Deaf or hard of hearing students. Explicit teaching is required and ensuring students have access to their technology when teaching these components is essential. In addition, students with Cochlear implants hear tone and pitch differently to hearing students. This needs to be noted when assessing students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing.

Teaching strategies

Berninger and Wolf (2016) and Gross (2017) indicate teachers should support students to develop oral language and communication skills using a range of strategies. These include:

  • reminding students to speak audibly where appropriate, including articulating words clearly
  • regular opportunities for targeted small group work
  • regular opportunities for structured conversations with teachers, other adults and peers
  • specific acknowledgement for listening skills
  • encouraging turn-taking
  • providing daily opportunities for sustained conversations, including using open-ended questions to extend interactions
  • expanding on students’ sentences and ideas
  • modelling the same content of a statement in a more academic and grammatically correct structure (known as recasting)
  • explicitly teaching concept words and academic vocabulary that may be unfamiliar to students (also see Teaching advice for Vocabulary)
  • modelling and guiding syntactic structure and sentence constructions (also see Teaching advice for Creating written texts)
  • maintaining and encouraging eye contact where appropriate
  • pausing after questions to allow time for students to develop an answer
  • asking students to summarise information communicated to them (also see Teaching advice for Stage 2 Reading comprehension /Teaching advice for Stage 3 Reading comprehension)
  • explaining and demonstrating the subtleties of intonation, stress and pace when speaking
  • using consistent cues that remind students to attend to listening and/or receiving information through AAC
  • explicitly teaching reading fluency (see Teaching advice for Stage 2 Reading fluency)
  • posing questions before, during and after a learning experience to check for understanding
  • establishing consistent rules and protocols for collaborative discussions.

When using these strategies to support students’ oral language and communication skills, it is important to be aware of language and cultural considerations. For example, eye contact may have different interpretations in some cultures, and some phonemes of English may be difficult to distinguish and reproduce.

Also refer to the teaching advice provided for Early Stage 1 and Stage 1 Oral language and communication focus area as the suggested strategies are relevant to all stages of learning.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students bring culturally varied skills, experiences, orientations and predispositions to learning. In the English syllabus, Oral language and communication is focused on developing and using Standard Australian English (SAE). It is important to recognise that developing proficiency in first languages supports language development in general. However, learning to use SAE allows students to participate in social and educational community interactions and enables them to develop as bilingual and multilingual learners who can codeswitch, using their language(s) and dialect(s) as appropriate (Gross 2017).

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6 and so some students at the Beginning and Emerging phase of language development may communicate using nonverbal gestures such as shrugs and head nods and/or use single words and/or high frequency words and expressions to communicate. Interpreting responses and modelling and recasting spoken language into academic language allows students to imitate and develop their oral communication skills.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Speaking and Listening modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Oral language and communication.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Oral Interaction level 6 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is creating written texts?

Writing is a social practice that requires sustained cognition. Writing proficiency is central to student success during the school years and post-school outcomes (Graham et al. 2019). The process and product of writing can be influenced by:

  • the writing environment
  • available writing tools
  • the writing topic
  • the purpose and audience for writing, including a writer’s intent
  • time devoted to the task of writing.

Creating written texts involves coordination of many elements and processes (Graham et al. 2019).

Proficient writers:

  • write for a purpose and consider their audience, even if it is just themselves
  • apply knowledge of a topic and its related vocabulary, and combine these with an understanding of genre when developing ideas for writing
  • craft a variety of sentence structures using knowledge of grammar and punctuation
  • use accurate spelling
  • fluently handwrite, type and/or use assistive technology confidently
  • select the most appropriate transcription tools for a writing task
  • make considered decisions about linguistic, visual, spatial and/or multimodal design elements to achieve a particular communicative goal
  • deliberately engage in processes for writing that include planning, monitoring and revising, which provides them opportunities to reflect on the quality of their texts.

Creating a written text is impacted by several core, interrelated factors (Hebert et al. 2016; Parkin 2021; Berninger et al. 2002; Hayes and Berninger 2014). According to Hebert et al. (2018), these include transcription skills (e.g. spelling and handwriting) and executive functioning skills (e.g. self-regulation, planning, organisation and self-monitoring), both of which enable text generation (e.g. ideation, word choice, sentence constructions and text structuring).

Image long description: Interrelated factors in writing include executive functioning, transcription and text generation, all of which are constrained by working memory. When the demand for working memory is increased for an aspect of writing, fewer resources are available to manage other aspects of writing.

As illustrated in Figure 1, executive functioning, transcription and text generation are all constrained by working memory. When the demand for working memory is increased for an aspect of writing (e.g. transcription), fewer resources are available to manage other aspects of writing.

Why is writing important?

Writing is valuable in societies around the world in many ways. Creating written texts is becoming increasingly synonymous with production and productivity in the workplace (Brandt 2015). While writing has been a key practice in many workplaces, more people are devoting increased time to writing in formal and informal communication contexts. Being able to create written texts:

  • enables learning and interactions
  • provides a means to invent, record and preserve experiences and histories
  • express emotions and opinions
  • inform, influence and persuade
  • build a sense of identity.

Writing can strengthen the process of acquiring new knowledge across different subjects and schooling years (Graham et al. 2020; Huerta and Garza 2019). For example, students may create summaries, descriptions or explanations for a topic of study. They may write to compare or connect information within topics or texts. They may take notes or develop graphic organisers and mind maps to support their learning of a topic. Writing about material that has been read can also improve comprehension of that material (Graham and Hebert 2011). Furthermore, explicitly teaching the elements of writing can improve word-level reading and reading fluency (Graham and Hebert 2011; Graham et al. 2019).

Considerations for teaching

The act of creating a written text, is a complex thinking process with many distinguishable elements, processes and stages. Even at single sentence level, it requires a student to: 

  • generate an idea 
  • retrieve the words that represent it 
  • arrange and rearrange the words mentally into a sequence that makes sense syntactically and semantically. 

These processes occur before and during writing, regardless of the mode in which a student presents a text. They may include rich discussions to elicit and plan ideas for writing and to reflect on texts when monitoring and revising (also see Teaching advice for Oral language and communication). 

Support students to improve their writing by:

  • nurturing a culture of writers across the school, where students write frequently for a range of meaningful audiences and purposes, and where writing is shared and valued
  • devoting increased amounts of time for students to write, ideally totalling at least one hour per day across different learning contexts
  • offering a range of writing contexts that include short and timed writing episodes as well as extended writing tasks where longer and more complex texts can be created over several days
  • ensuring explicit strategy instruction is included, focusing on planning, sequencing, creating, revising, editing and publishing texts
  • modelling and encouraging the use of graphic organisers when planning to create a text
  • co-constructing and using word banks to support students’ language choices when writing
  • providing opportunities for students to create texts using print tools (e.g. pen and paper) as well as digital writing tools
  • providing explicit and carefully scaffolded instruction, ensuring a balance between sentence-level writing and compositional writing
  • providing opportunities for students to write informative, persuasive and imaginative texts on a wide range of topics across learning areas
  • teaching the macrostructure and microstructure of texts through examining mentor (exemplar) texts, modelling the writing, and guided and shared writing practices
  • expanding their content knowledge across learning areas, as well as their linguistic and vocabulary knowledge through integrating reading and writing
  • embedding the explicit teaching of grammar and punctuation in meaningful writing tasks
  • seizing ‘teachable moments’ to reinforce spelling, grammar and punctuation expectations
  • providing additional and scaffolded teaching for students with learning difficulties and disabilities
  • embedding frequent formative assessment and providing explicit, achievable feedback that instils agency within the student
  • providing opportunities for students to plan writing ideas in their home language if needed and scaffold the students through the editing process to transfer text into Standard Australian English.

Supporting students who are unable to use handwriting when creating written texts

Some students may need access to alternative transcription formats and assistive technologies to create written texts.

These may include:

  • text-to-speech devices
  • speech-to-text devices
  • keyboard or switch devices
  • AAC devices
  • communication boards
  • symbol-making software
  • word-prediction software.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6. Students in the Beginning and Emerging phases of language development may have some experience of writing in their home language(s) or dialect(s) and will require scaffolding and explicit targeted support to demonstrate achievement. Students in these phases may demonstrate some sound–letter awareness and awareness of left to right directionality. They may also communicate in a small range of familiar words, or through drawings and symbols. Students may also dictate ideas that can be scribed by teachers or peers.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Creating written texts.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Writing level 5 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

A scaffolded instructional approach

The figure below offers one illustration of how levels of support may shift, depending on the needs of students, when implementing a scaffolded approach to writing. For example, some students may require higher levels of support at a particular phase in the writing process.

Image long description: In 3–6, a scaffolded approach to teaching writing is cyclic. It includes modelled teaching, shared teaching, guided teaching and independent learning. The cycle may occur when building the field for writing, analysing mentor texts, planning, drafting, monitoring, revising and editing texts.

Refer to the Additional teaching advice, Early Stage 1 – Creating written texts and Additional teaching advice, Stage 1 – Creating written texts for descriptions of various teaching strategies. The information provided includes:

  • modelled writing
  • shared writing or co-construction
  • interactive writing
  • guided writing
  • independent writing
  • classroom environments that support writing success
  • mentor texts.

What is handwriting and digital transcription?

Transcription skills involve handwriting and using digital tools to produce text.

Handwriting is the formation, size, spacing, position and placement of alphabetic letters on a page.

Handwriting fluency includes being able to efficiently write legible letters from memory using adequate hand and hand–eye skills, such as fine motor abilities.

Using digital transcription tools for creating written texts includes being able to locate and use software functionalities and efficiently navigate the keyboard to type words with ease.

Why are they important?

Developing a fluent and legible handwriting style as well as fluent typing/word processing are essential skills for text creation. If handwriting or typing is automatic and fast, the writer can concentrate on other elements of writing. The development of fluent and accurate transcription skills, through both handwriting and digital technologies, can free up working memory so that attention can be devoted to other important aspects of text creation (Medwell and Wray 2007).

Given the established benefits of sensory–motor integration when handwriting, it is vital to continue handwriting instruction in Years 3 to 6 (Askvik et al. 2020).

Handwriting facilitates word learning because the kinaesthetic action of the hand contributes to greater recognition and memorisation of word-specific spelling (Longcamp et al. 2005).

Research has further demonstrated that handwriting letters of the alphabet or copying text under timed conditions is causally related to compositional writing quality (Graham et al. 2000). Handwriting is an important skill for tasks such as note-taking, which in turn supports learning, and conceptualisation and retention of information (Mueller and Oppenheimer 2014).

To support students in developing skills to communicative effectively in an interactive multimedia world, it is essential to explicitly teach students how to use digital technologies (Crocket et al. 2011). Students need to learn how to use digital technologies for a range of communicative tasks including emailing, creating digital texts, or drafting and editing extended pieces of writing, including multimodal texts.

Supporting students who are unable to use handwriting

Some students may need access to alternative transcription formats and assistive technologies instead of handwriting. These may include: 

  • speech-to-text devices 
  • keyboard or switch devices 
  • AAC devices.

Considerations for teaching

Teaching handwriting

Support students to develop handwriting skills by:

  • ensuring students have consolidated appropriate letter formation and pencil grasp before introducing joined letters
  • clearly demonstrating letter formation including how to join letters using a cursive writing style
  • providing explicit teaching followed by short daily practice sessions. Short, sharp and frequent handwriting lessons are likely to be more effective than longer, less regular lessons
  • explaining how to join letters, accompanied by modelling
  • encouraging students to immediately practise the modelled handwriting and encourage self-talk as letter-joining is practised
  • providing opportunities for students to practise at tables and chairs and in workbooks so they can adopt the posture needed for fluent and sustained writing
  • noticing and providing explicit feedback on accurate letter formation
  • scaffolding the learning by allowing students to progress from observing a model, to copying and then writing from memory
  • encouraging students to evaluate their own handwriting after practising – for example, asking them to circle the word that they believe is formed very well
  • enabling students with established cursive handwriting to develop a personal handwriting style. A cursive looped style may also be adopted.

Teachers can also support students to develop a cursive handwriting style by demonstrating key features of joining letters. For example:

Diagonal joins

  • used to join the next letter at the top of the letter’s body
  • used to join to the next letter at a 45-degree angle.

Horizontal joins

  • used to join after the letters o, r, v, w and x.

Notice a slight dip in the horizontal join:

Retrace the top of an anti-clockwise letter following a horizontal join:

No joins

  • no join is needed after the letters b, f, g, j, p, s and y.

Pen(cil) lift and drop

  • supports movement of the hand and letter spacing
  • helps to minimise retracing of letters that are joined, especially with the letters a, c, d, g and q.

Teachers may also use visual aids such as lined paper (e.g. ‘dotted thirds’) to support students in developing consistent size and spacing. As students gain increased control and fluency, the width between the lines is narrowed and the provision of handwriting aids may be reduced or removed when handwriting is fluent and consistent in size and spacing.

Teachers may also need to support students to develop handwriting skills through provision of additional daily revision and consolidation time, and/or through a range of adaptive tools. Keyboard or other assistive technology skills may need to be considered as an alternative if a student is unable to meet the physical demands of handwriting (Handley-More et al. 2003).

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

As not all languages are alphabetic and/or may have different scripts some students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) at the Beginning and Emerging phases of language development may not be familiar with the formation of letters, upper and lower case and left to right directionality of Standard Australian English (SAE).

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Handwriting.

Teaching digital transcription

Support students to develop digital transcription skills by:

  • teaching touch typing skills
  • teaching students how to use software functions, including shortcuts, to support digital text creation
  • valuing accuracy of typing over speed
  • providing opportunities for students to frequently practise at tables and chairs, ensuring devices are positioned at a height and angle that supports ergonomic device-use and clear vision
  • knowing that keys on the keyboard are placed differently in other languages.

Additional opportunities for guided and independent practice may be required, in the classroom or through specific interventions. Decisions about adjustments for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

What is reading comprehension?

Reading comprehension is an active process of problem-solving and critical thinking about texts. It relies on the ability to recognise most or all words in a text. Although word reading is necessary for reading comprehension, it is not sufficient (Oakhill et al. 2014).

To understand texts, proficient readers draw on:

  • background knowledge
  • vocabulary knowledge
  • knowledge of text structures.

They make connections to support their understanding by integrating new information with old information while reading.

Proficient readers:

  • know why they are reading
  • understand the purpose of a text
  • know that imaginative, informative and persuasive texts have different structures and features
  • understand the various conventions relating to types of texts
  • adapt their reading according to a particular purpose, mode and medium
  • monitor their comprehension.

Comprehension of a text occurs as the reader builds a mental representation (mental model) of a message from the text (Perfetti and Stafura 2014). Reading comprehension also includes being able to identify, describe, explain and interpret how multimodal elements are used in texts to convey meaning.

Why is it important?

Understanding a wide range of texts is central to the study of English. Reading comprehension can make reading enjoyable and informative. It enables diverse perspectives to be considered, and informed decisions to be made. Reading comprehension is needed to succeed in school, work and life in general.

Students in Stages 2 and 3 continue to build understanding of increasingly complex texts so that they can enjoy texts and learn across all subjects. For example, in Science, students read to learn facts on natural phenomena. In Mathematics, word problems that students read need to be understood to be solved. In History, students study texts that describe events throughout history. In the Arts, reading can inspire creativity in art making.

Reading comprehension and writing mutually reinforce one another and rely on similar thinking processes. Given this reciprocity between reading and writing, comprehension of a text deepens when reading and writing activities are regularly integrated in the classroom. Reading comprehension is a critical skill that helps students to plan for writing as well as read and revise their own writing.

Considerations for teaching

Supporting all students’ understanding that the goal for reading must involve a clear, complete and integrated mental model of the text is of utmost importance when teaching reading comprehension. Students who experience difficulties with their reading may not generate enough inferences to ensure adequate comprehension and will not have the flexibility to adjust their reading styles to meet different task aims. Therefore, they will often view reading as a decoding activity. Proficient readers, on the other hand, will view reading as a meaning making activity, be flexible with their reading styles and will take time to read and study a text to extract essential information. Consistent goals for reading, with appropriate support for specific students is key.

The complexity of texts varies in terms of vocabulary, syntactic complexity, content and the arrangement or structure of ideas. To support a student’s reading comprehension, careful text selection is crucial because the extent to which specific component reading skills contribute to comprehension will vary depending on textual demands (Kim 2020).

The complexity and length of texts that students encounter will increase in Stages 2 and 3. Therefore, the skills and strategies that support students’ comprehension of texts will also continue to develop.

It is important for teachers to frequently monitor their students’ comprehension when they are reading. While students decode words in a text, the language can be complex, and deep understanding of the language can be difficult to grasp. Texts that students will encounter in Stages 2 and 3 include increasingly complex, multisyllabic words. It is important to continue to build students’ decoding and encoding skills so they can read complex multisyllabic words. For Stage 2, this can be addressed in parallel with Reading fluency as well as in the phonological component of Spelling. For Stage 3, fluency instruction continues as part of reading comprehension instruction, and can also be addressed in parallel with Spelling.

Students may need additional support in comprehension. Developing and connecting background knowledge is important in making sense of what is read (Zwiers 2010). This can be supported through techniques such as predictions, visualisation, concept posters, text organisers or thinking structures such as Know – Want to know – Learned.

Other students may need further support to be able to access and understand texts. This could include specialised literacy intervention, or assistive technology such as:

  • text-to-speech devices, such as a screen reader
  • audiobooks
  • optical character recognition.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6. These students may still be learning the basic features of English print such as directionality and letter–sound relationships. Other students may arrive with limited English proficiency and some literacy and reading comprehension skills in their home language. These students can draw on their existing knowledge and experiences to help them read in English. For EAL/D learners at the Beginning and Emerging phases of language development the complexity and length of texts needs to be challenging and age appropriate but not beyond the students’ current ability. As reading requires decoding as well as conceptual and cultural background knowledge; this background and field knowledge needs to be explicitly taught so that students are able to comprehend the texts.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Reading/viewing mode of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s learning needs in relation to Reading comprehension.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding level 5 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.
