What is oral language and communication?

Oral language refers to speaking (expressive language skills) and listening (receptive language skills) and is inherently social (Gee 2011).

Oral language develops knowledge of how language is used in context. Varied opportunities for oral language use in a range of contexts allows students to observe, understand and practise different language experiences for a range of purposes and audiences.

Communication encompasses a system of both reception and expression, as well as translation of spoken words and use of nonverbal communication modes such as gesture. Some students may need to develop skills in using augmentative and alternative forms of communication (AAC) to supplement or replace oral language. AACs can be unaided or aided. Unaided AACs include gestures, facial expressions and signs, such as Key Word Sign. Aided AACs include symbols, objects, pictures and voice output communication aids. The most appropriate AAC should be considered for each student. Some students may also use a combination of communication forms.

Oral language and communication should be embedded in learning experiences across a wide range of subject areas. They are supported by the environment, opportunities and interactions of language learning (Gross 2017).

Why is it important?

Oral language supports vocabulary learning and builds background knowledge. Background knowledge supports reading comprehension. Poor reading comprehension may indicate a need to further develop language comprehension. Furthermore, a student’s reading comprehension can often be constrained by their listening comprehension (Biemiller 2003). Therefore, teachers should support students to establish robust listening comprehension skills. Oral language is used when planning and creating written texts to support ideation, vocabulary and grammar. Receptive and expressive oral language skills have been found to relate directly to written text creation (Kim and Scatschneider 2017).

The oral language that students engage with becomes increasingly complex in Stages 2 and 3. Some vocabulary they encounter may be less familiar and sentences may be longer and harder to process semantically and syntactically. Students are also expected to make connections and inferences across longer stretches of language. Bridging the gap between a student’s everyday oral language and academic language is critical. This is particularly important for students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) as many EAL/D learners develop their oral language skills faster than their academic language skills (Cummins 2008).

Considerations for teaching

The most important initial step in developing a student’s oral language and communication is to understand students’ skills at the start of Stage 2, so that teaching begins at the point(s) of need. The content groups, Interacting, Listening for understanding and Presenting, will provide guidance for this.

Oral language and communication can be addressed in parallel with other focus areas. For example, when addressing:

  • vocabulary, students learn and use new words through dialogic communications facilitated by the teacher. This can ensure students are exposed to and use language for a range of purposes and audiences, which will help them to identify how language changes in different contexts
  • reading fluency, students apply taught skills such as intonation and stress during oral reading and when presenting
  • creating written texts, students participate in focused discussions when planning their written texts, or when incorporating multimodal elements into a prepared spoken presentation
  • understanding and responding to literature, students discuss textual structures, features and how literature engages them.

It is important students understand the difference between talk as a process, e.g. a discussion in a group setting to develop comprehension and talk as production e.g. speeches, and how oral language differs in these contexts.

Students with complex communication needs

Students with complex communication needs may have different levels of receptive and expressive communication. Students who primarily communicate using nonverbal language need to be supported to develop communication skills using their preferred communication form(s). Some students’ preferred receptive communication form(s) may be different to their preferred expressive communication form(s). The syllabus has included Complementary content to assist teachers to support students who use alternative communication forms. For more information refer to the NESA website.

Tone, pitch and volume can be hard to distinguish for d/Deaf or hard of hearing students. Explicit teaching is required and ensuring students have access to their technology when teaching these components is essential. In addition, students with Cochlear implants hear tone and pitch differently to hearing students. This needs to be noted when assessing students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing.

Teaching strategies

Berninger and Wolf (2016) and Gross (2017) indicate teachers should support students to develop oral language and communication skills using a range of strategies. These include:

  • reminding students to speak audibly where appropriate, including articulating words clearly
  • regular opportunities for targeted small group work
  • regular opportunities for structured conversations with teachers, other adults and peers
  • specific acknowledgement for listening skills
  • encouraging turn-taking
  • providing daily opportunities for sustained conversations, including using open-ended questions to extend interactions
  • expanding on students’ sentences and ideas
  • modelling the same content of a statement in a more academic and grammatically correct structure (known as recasting)
  • explicitly teaching concept words and academic vocabulary that may be unfamiliar to students (also see Teaching advice for Vocabulary)
  • modelling and guiding syntactic structure and sentence constructions (also see Teaching advice for Creating written texts)
  • maintaining and encouraging eye contact where appropriate
  • pausing after questions to allow time for students to develop an answer
  • asking students to summarise information communicated to them (also see Teaching advice for Reading comprehension)
  • explaining and demonstrating the subtleties of intonation, stress and pace when speaking
  • using consistent cues that remind students to attend to listening and/or receiving information through AAC
  • explicitly teaching reading fluency (see Teaching advice for Reading fluency)
  • posing questions before, during and after a learning experience to check for understanding
  • establishing consistent rules and protocols for collaborative discussions.

When using these strategies to support students’ oral language and communication skills, it is important to be aware of language and cultural considerations. For example, eye contact may have different interpretations in some cultures, and some phonemes of English may be difficult to distinguish and reproduce.

Also refer to the teaching advice provided for Early Stage 1 and Stage 1 Oral language and communication focus area as the suggested strategies are relevant to all stages of learning.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students bring culturally varied skills, experiences, orientations and predispositions to learning. In the English syllabus, Oral language and communication is focused on developing and using Standard Australian English (SAE). It is important to recognise that developing proficiency in first languages supports language development in general. However, learning to use SAE allows students to participate in social and educational community interactions and enables them to develop as bilingual and multilingual learners who can code-switch, using their language(s) and dialect(s) as appropriate (Gross 2017).

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6. Some students at the Beginning and Emerging phase of language development may communicate using nonverbal gestures such as shrugs and head nods and/or use single words and/or high frequency words and expressions to communicate. Interpreting responses and modelling and recasting spoken language into academic language allows students to imitate and develop their oral communication skills.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Speaking and Listening modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Oral language and communication.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Oral Interaction levels 7 and 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is reading comprehension?

Reading comprehension is an active process of problem-solving and critical thinking about texts. It relies on the ability to recognise most or all words in a text. Although word reading is necessary for reading comprehension, it is not sufficient (Oakhill et al. 2014).

To understand texts, proficient readers draw on:

  • background knowledge
  • vocabulary knowledge
  • knowledge of text structures.

They make connections to support their understanding by integrating new information with old information while reading.

Proficient readers:

  • know why they are reading
  • understand the purpose of a text
  • know that imaginative, informative and persuasive texts have different structures and features
  • understand the various conventions relating to types of texts
  • adapt their reading according to a particular purpose, mode and medium
  • monitor their comprehension.

Comprehension of a text occurs as the reader builds a mental representation (mental model) of a message from the text (Perfetti and Stafura 2014). Reading comprehension also includes being able to identify, describe, explain and interpret how multimodal elements are used in texts to convey meaning.

Why is it important?

Understanding a wide range of texts is central to the study of English. Reading comprehension can make reading enjoyable and informative. It enables diverse perspectives to be considered, and informed decisions to be made. Reading comprehension is needed to succeed in school, work and life in general.

Students in Stages 2 and 3 continue to build understanding of increasingly complex texts so that they can enjoy texts and learn across all subjects. For example, in Science, students read to learn facts on natural phenomena. In Mathematics, word problems that students read need to be understood to be solved. In History, students study texts that describe events throughout history. In the Arts, reading can inspire creativity in art making.

Reading comprehension and writing mutually reinforce one another and rely on similar thinking processes. Given this reciprocity between reading and writing, comprehension of a text deepens when reading and writing activities are regularly integrated in the classroom. Reading comprehension is a critical skill that helps students to plan for writing as well as read and revise their own writing.

Supporting fluency development in Stage 3

Teaching and monitoring fluency does not cease at the end of Stage 2. By establishing and embedding routines and strategies for reading fluency in Stage 2, teachers should continue to support students’ reading fluency as part of a holistic approach to reading instruction in Stage 3 and beyond.

Considerations for teaching

Supporting all students’ understanding that the goal for reading must involve a clear, complete and integrated mental model of the text is of utmost importance when teaching reading comprehension. Students who experience difficulties with their reading may not generate enough inferences to ensure adequate comprehension and will not have the flexibility to adjust their reading styles to meet different task aims. Therefore, they will often view reading as a decoding activity. Proficient readers, on the other hand, will view reading as a meaning making activity, be flexible with their reading styles and will take time to read and study a text to extract essential information. Consistent goals for reading, with appropriate support for specific students is key.

The complexity of texts varies in terms of vocabulary, syntactic complexity, content and the arrangement or structure of ideas. To support a student’s reading comprehension, careful text selection is crucial because the extent to which specific component reading skills contribute to comprehension will vary depending on textual demands (Kim 2020).

The complexity and length of texts that students encounter will increase in Stages 2 and 3. Therefore, the skills and strategies that support students’ comprehension of texts will also continue to develop.

It is important for teachers to frequently monitor their students’ comprehension when they are reading. While students decode words in a text, the language can be complex, and deep understanding of the language can be difficult to grasp. Texts that students will encounter in Stages 2 and 3 include increasingly complex, multisyllabic words. It is important to continue to build students’ decoding and encoding skills so they can read complex multisyllabic words. For Stage 2, this can be addressed in parallel with Reading fluency as well as in the phonological component of Spelling. For Stage 3, fluency instruction continues as part of reading comprehension instruction, and can also be addressed in parallel with Spelling.

Students may need additional support in comprehension. Developing and connecting background knowledge is important in making sense of what is read (Zwiers 2010). This can be supported through techniques such as predictions, visualisation, concept posters, text organisers or thinking structures such as Know – Want to know – Learned.

Other students may need further support to be able to access and understand texts. This could include specialised literacy intervention, or assistive technology such as:

  • text-to-speech devices, such as a screen reader
  • audiobooks
  • optical character recognition.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6. These students may still be learning the basic features of English print such as directionality and letter–sound relationships. Other students may arrive with limited English proficiency and some literacy and reading comprehension skills in their home language. These students can draw on their existing knowledge and experiences to help them read in English. For EAL/D learners at the Beginning and Emerging phases of language development the complexity and length of texts needs to be challenging and age appropriate but not beyond the students’ current ability. As reading requires decoding as well as conceptual and cultural knowledge this background and field knowledge needs to be explicitly taught so that students are able to comprehend the texts.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Reading/viewing mode of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s learning needs in relation to Reading comprehension.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding levels 6 and 7 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

Why is it important?

Proficiency in spelling can influence how effectively a student creates written texts (Hayes and Berninger 2014). Spelling is the essential bridge between idea generation and text creation (Abbott et al. 2010). If too much attention is placed on spelling while creating texts, it can be difficult to devote cognitive attention to other important aspects of writing. Spelling ability can also compromise the precision and variety of words used when writing (Sumner et al. 2016).

If a student knows a word but is unsure how to spell the word, they are less likely to use it when creating a written text. The process of spelling words (rather than just reading words) can also help to establish long-term memory of word-specific representations, and in turn supports the development of word reading efficiency (Conrad et al. 2019).

Spelling instruction in Years 3 to 6 enables students to build their vocabulary knowledge and refine linguistic understandings of word structures.

Considerations for teaching

Explicit instruction in spelling is essential. Increasing explicit instruction can lead to sustained improvements in spelling, as well as writing and reading more broadly (Graham et al. 2012; Graham and Santangelo 2014). Spelling should not be taught through visual memorisation of whole words and repetitive drill (Berninger and Fayol 2008).

Some students may find the link between phonemes and graphemes more difficult to establish and will need extra time and repetition to consolidate these skills.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6. Students at the Beginning and Emerging phase of language development may have limited or no exposure to print literacy in their home language(s) or dialect(s) and be unfamiliar with spelling conventions. Some students will also come from countries where the home language(s) or dialect(s) have little or no written tradition or from cultures where the language is not alphabetic. Teachers may need to refer to Early Stage 1 and Stage 1 teaching advice.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Spelling.

What is literature?

The study of literature is central to the subject English. Literature studied in Stages 2 and 3 includes a wide range of fiction and nonfiction texts from diverse contemporary, historical and cultural contexts, in both print and digital forms. Wide study of literature enables students to share experiences about and beyond their lives. It can help to foster empathy, encourage critical thinking and nurture enjoyment of reading.

The Text requirements outline the variety of texts that students must engage with. They provide an important instructional guide for text selection.

Why is understanding and responding to literature important?

The study of literature supports students’ reading and writing skills through learning syntax, discourse and vocabulary. It enables students to develop an understanding of how authors craft sentences and structure text in purposeful and effective ways. Studying literature provides opportunities for students to engage in sustained discussions, fostering the development of oral language and vocabulary knowledge. Through close and wide reading of literature, students explore a range of familiar and new experiences, times, places, people and cultures.

The quality and range of literature students engage with is important in supporting their development of writing and reading skills (Duke et al. 2011). Students need opportunities for wide and close reading to see how language creates meaning and to consider different ways of thinking, thus broadening their context. These encounters offer access to unfamiliar ideas and introduce different vocabulary and sentence structures. The breadth and depth of quality literature studied by students can foster an appreciation of literature and pleasure in reading.

Reading, writing and oral language connections

Reading, writing and oral language are reciprocally related and mutually support and enhance one another (Berninger et al. 2002; Graham and Hebert 2011; Parodi 2007; Abbott et al. 2010; Kim and Scatschneider 2017). Writing about a text that is read can also help to build a richer representation of the content of a text (Duke et al. 2011; Graham and Hebert 2011). In addition, writing and engaging in structured conversations about literature can actively involve students in learning, as they are encouraged to identify and articulate what is relevant in a text, as well as reflect upon and evaluate what they read. Stage 2 and 3 students should discuss texts together to develop coherent and critical understandings.

Concepts in texts

Students should be given regular opportunities to engage with a variety of literature that includes strong examples of:

  • narrative
  • characterisation
  • imagery, symbol and connotation
  • genre
  • theme
  • perspective and context
  • argument and authority.

These concepts can be used as lenses through which to study literature.

Text selection for the instructional purpose is important. For example, a poem may lend itself to teaching the concepts of imagery, symbol and connotation, while an advertisement or speech may be suitable for teaching the concepts of argument and authority.

Mentor texts

Literature should be used to exemplify what is possible in terms of how specific concepts can contribute to understanding a text. A mentor text is a quality text that clearly demonstrates the qualities of a concept.

Mentor texts can show students how effective writing looks, sounds and how it demands a response from the audience. Students analyse and explore the ways mentor texts can be used for imitation as they develop an independent style.

As students read texts closely, they begin to read like a writer, building knowledge about how authors select textual structures and features to convey effects and relationships for different purposes (McDonald 2018).

Guided discussion

Guided discussion about a text is an important teaching strategy to support higher-order comprehension and interpretation of texts. It enables students to understand the interactions of textual features and ideas, that they can then use or adapt when creating their own texts.

Guided discussion uses refined questioning and thinking aloud by the teacher across multiple interactions with a text. It involves inviting students to pose questions and elaborate on responses.

Rich dialogic discussion about literature can yield many benefits to students (Edwards-Groves 2014). For example, it can:

  • promote creative, imaginative thinking
  • reveal understandings and misunderstandings
  • help clarify thinking
  • build confidence
  • support learning and memory
  • promote reasoning and critical thinking
  • be used to scaffold language development
  • nourish the development of social and emotional skills.

Considerations for teaching

Understanding and responding to literature provides opportunities for students to:

  • study a wide variety of texts in different modes
  • discuss the relationship between images and language and how they work together to support meaning
  • use metalanguage to identify and discuss structures and features in texts
  • identify and discuss how authors and illustrators use language and images for a particular purpose and audience, and deliberately use and innovate on those when creating texts
  • understand and analyse the personal, social and cultural contexts and perspectives represented in texts
  • discuss author style in texts
  • take part in supportive discussion structures such as Think-Pair-Share
  • make use of ‘wait time’ when needed to offer a considered response
  • actively engage in sustained conversations by posing and responding to open-ended questions and follow-up questions (e.g. ‘what else do you know about …?’)
  • rephrase or build upon another person’s ideas using their own words.

Some students may need further support to be able to access and understand texts. This could include specialised literacy intervention, and assistive technology such as:

  • text-to-speech devices such as a screen reader
  • audiobooks
  • optical character recognition.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6. Some students at the Beginning and Emerging phase of language development may therefore require explicit support and scaffolding to decode and understand print texts. Students with limited literacy background may be unfamiliar with books and require explicit teaching of directionality, print marks and English print conventions. These students may use book illustrations to support their understanding and respond to literature with images, symbols or their home language(s) or dialect(s). Some students at this phase of English development may be familiar with identifying the structures, features, purpose and context of texts in their home language(s) or dialect(s). They may thus require frontloading of specific vocabulary and metalanguage to demonstrate their understanding and participate in sustained conversations about the texts.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Understanding and responding to literature.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding levels 6 and 7, Writing levels 6 and 7 and Oral interaction levels 7 and 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is vocabulary?

Vocabulary refers to words that students can recognise, understand and use for communication. A large and rich vocabulary is often regarded as a hallmark of education, with strong relationships to reading and school achievement. Vocabulary knowledge supports students to recognise humour in wordplay and brings precision to spoken and written uses for language.

Vocabulary is closely related to reading comprehension – for any reading of a text, the extent of a reader’s word knowledge is crucial for comprehension. Accurate and fast retrieval of word meanings unburdens working memory and allows the brain to connect words into sentences, and sentences into larger passages of text.

Vocabulary knowledge is comprised of 3 highly related but distinct dimensions (Kieffer and Lesaux 2012): 

  • breadth: the number of words a person knows 
  • contextual sensitivity: the different meanings for words when used in different contexts
  • morphological awareness: an understanding that prefixes and suffixes can be added or taken away to change the meaning of a word.

Syllabus content in English 3–6 is listed in content groups, Learning and using words and Defining and analysing words, to reflect the 3 dimensions of vocabulary. While much vocabulary is learnt by students without formal teaching (for example, through conversation, observation, television, other media and reading), a wide range of research shows that explicitly teaching vocabulary can measurably improve learning. This is particularly true for reading comprehension, if the necessary and appropriate words in texts are taught well.

Once students can read proficiently, usually at approximately 9 or 10 years, written language becomes the dominant source for learning vocabulary, while in earlier years, this predominantly occurs through spoken language opportunities (Sternberg 1987; Nippold 2016). 

Building students’ vocabulary knowledge goes beyond knowing the definition of a word. It encompasses knowledge of the different contextual meanings of a word, shades of meaning of a word, semantic associations, and knowledge of its morphological forms. Robust vocabulary instruction can enhance language comprehension and production, and involves (Beck et al. 2013):

  • discussing detailed information about words and their uses
  • frequent and varied opportunities for students to think about and use words.

Three tiers of vocabulary knowledge

The Tiers of vocabulary provide a framework to understand the types of words that require instructional attention (Beck et al. 2013).

Tier 1 words typically appear in oral conversations and so children are exposed to them at high frequency from a very early age. With this exposure, children become readily familiar with these words. Tier 1 includes basic-level, everyday words, e.g. dog, baby, happy, pretty, was, come, said. While we need to teach students how to read and write these words, they rarely require instruction at school in terms of meaning and use.

Tier 2 words are general academic words that can be used across a variety of domains. They are of high utility for mature language users and are commonly used in written language, e.g. contradict, precede, stale, awful, snuggle. Tier 2 words add power and precision to written and spoken language, but many Tier 2 words are most commonly found in written language and explicit teaching of these words is recommended.

Tier 3 words are technical words that are used in specific situations, e.g. decibel, cataclysm, atom, quaver. These are best learnt in a content area, domain or discipline.

The Three tiers of vocabulary posters: English K–6 are available as one downloadable document to support teachers’ and students’ understanding of vocabulary.

Why is it important?

Research highlights the importance of planned vocabulary instruction in all learning areas (Baker et al. 1995). Vocabulary acquisition is crucial for student’s academic development, as they require a rich body of word knowledge, including specialised vocabulary to learn content area material. Therefore, effective strategies for helping students understand both common words used in uncommon ways, and specialised vocabulary across all learning areas are of utmost importance.

A situation that sees limited opportunities to practise expressive language before starting school can restrict the vocabulary of children and make it challenging to attain an adequate vocabulary at school. Research involving young students experiencing disadvantage has shown that those students can experience particular difficulty defining abstract, academic, literary and less common words (i.e. Tier 2 and Tier 3 words) compared with students representing a normative population (Monster et al. 2021).

Considerations for teaching

Explicit teaching of vocabulary in learning areas is essential. Vocabulary development requires repeated exposures to new words, learning definitional and contextual information about those words and engagement in active, deep learning experiences (Kieffer and Lesaux 2012).

A robust approach to teaching vocabulary in Stage 2 and Stage 3 can support students to: 

  • become word conscious and build interest in learning new words 
  • read widely to learn new words, and build their productive oral and written vocabularies 
  • include academic or discipline-specific words in spoken and written language, to enhance authority (breadth) 
  • understand that words can have multiple meanings and that word meanings can vary with context
  • select appropriate words for a text’s purpose when writing
  • explore meanings of words across multiple contexts 
  • source and discuss word definitions and redefine those definitions 
  • develop understanding of the contextual sensitivity of words (understand subtle shades of meaning – semantics)  
  • study etymology (learn the history of words) 
  • learn the meaning of morphemes and how they change meaning in words.

Please see the additional teaching advice for Vocabulary.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) enter school at any time in Years 3–6. Thus, some students at the Beginning and Emerging phase of language development may have substantial vocabulary in their home language(s) or dialect(s) but need additional support to develop vocabulary in Standard Australian English (SAE). Making connections with their vocabulary in their home language(s) or dialect(s) can support their vocabulary learning in SAE.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Reading/viewing, Writing, Speaking and Listening modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Vocabulary.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding levels 6 and 7, Writing levels 6 and 7, and Oral Interaction levels 7 and 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is Expressing ideas and composing texts?

Students compose texts that express and represent their ideas, experiences, perspectives, knowledge and understanding gained from engagement with texts.

These skills and strategies are developed through exploring: the functional components of writing, representing and speaking; the stylistic elements that shape meaning in the creation of texts in a wide range of forms, media and modes, including written, aural, visual and multimodal texts; and the process of composition, including planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers should provide students with a broad range of opportunities to compose texts by designing learning experiences that include a range of modes, including multimodal responses.

How do I assess this focus area?

The outcomes for this focus area should be assessed in conjunction with outcomes from other focus areas. This assessment should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate.

Using the content, teachers can assess students’ development of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills required for expressing ideas and composing texts. Some students with disability may require adjustments when composing texts.

Students' progress can be observed when they are expressing ideas through the composition of texts.  Students should be provided with multiple opportunities to demonstrate their knowledge, understanding and skills in planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting on their work.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

All students will benefit from explicit modelling of the grammatical codes and conventions of writing in Standard Australian English (SAE) as well as the language structures and vocabulary required to compose a range of texts. This will be a particularly useful strategy for students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D). Some EAL/D learners may experience a silent period, and may benefit from having access to visual and bilingual supports when expressing ideas orally. Modelling of pronunciation and intonation will support students to develop oral fluency.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Expressing ideas and composing texts A.

Teachers can use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding level 7, Writing level 7 and Oral interaction level 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is Reading, viewing and listening to texts?

Students read, view and listen to texts through comprehension, inference and analysis. They engage with these texts for meaning, and for challenge, interest and enjoyment. It is important that students have a breadth of reading experiences in Stage 4 to assist them to produce high quality writing.

Students develop their metacognitive skills to reflect on reading and develop into active and independent readers and learners.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers should provide students with a broad range of opportunities to engage with texts in a variety of forms, and from a variety of media and technologies, such as through the study of selected extracts of a text, the extended study of specific texts, or independent reading. Texts should be selected in accordance with the 7–10 text requirements, provide an appropriate level of challenge, and be accessible for all students.

How do I assess this focus area?

The outcome for this focus area should be assessed in conjunction with outcomes from other focus areas. This assessment should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate.

Using the content, teachers can assess students’ development of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills required for reading, viewing and listening to texts. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access and respond to texts.

Students' progress can be observed when they express an understanding of texts with which they have engaged. Understanding can be expressed in many forms, including through incorporating home languages or dialects.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Explicit teaching of vocabulary, cultural references and context will support all students to engage with the ideas, perspectives and values represented in texts. These strategies will be particularly useful in supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D). Modelling pace, tone and pronunciation, and providing frequent opportunities to practise reading aloud, can support development of students’ reading fluency. When reading for interest and enjoyment and when reflecting on the experience of reading, students may benefit from first expressing ideas and opinions in their home language(s) and/or dialect(s) to support consolidation of understanding.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in Listening, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Reading, viewing and listening to texts. 

Teachers can use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding level 7 and Oral interaction level 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is Understanding and responding to texts?

As the central focus of learning in English, students develop their knowledge and understanding of texts in order to compose responses in a range of modes and for a range of contexts, purposes and audiences.

Students learn to understand and respond to texts through exploring how textual forms and features, aesthetic qualities, voice, and structural components of texts, represent ideas and values. They develop an understanding of how texts from different historical, social and cultural contexts may challenge or reflect the values and perspectives of groups and individuals. They also build an understanding of how texts can be understood in relation to one another.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers should design learning experiences that require students to consider how forms and features of texts shape the representation of ideas and values, and connections and relationships, and how meaning is conveyed in the texts of others and in their own texts.

How do I assess this focus area?

The outcomes for this focus area should be assessed in conjunction with outcomes from other focus areas. This assessment should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate.

Using the content, teachers can assess students’ development of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills required for understanding and responding to texts. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access and respond to texts.

Students' progress can be observed when they are engaging with the ideas, perspectives and values in texts, and how these are communicated and understood. Students can demonstrate their understanding through written, spoken, visual and multimodal responses. Where the mode of response has been prescribed by the teacher, this should not preclude students from using their preferred communication form(s). Assessment of this focus area should consider the texts of others and students’ own texts.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Explicit teaching of vocabulary, cultural references and context will support all students to engage with the ideas, perspectives and values represented in texts. Modelling of the metalanguage required to communicate about narrative conventions, and how language forms and features shape meaning will support students to respond to and demonstrate their understanding of texts. These will be particularly useful strategies for supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D). EAL/D learners may benefit from using their home language(s) and/or dialect(s) when reflecting on how texts represent personal and collective identities, values and experiences and when generating their responses to texts.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Understanding and responding to texts A.

Teachers can use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding level 7, Writing level 7 and Oral interaction level 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

What is Communicating?

The focus area Communicating is unique to English 7–10 Life Skills and describes the skills required to engage and connect with others in familiar and unfamiliar contexts, and everyday environments. Students develop skills in responding to cues, expressing their own preferences and emotions, and engaging in simple interactions, including initiating interactions.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area can be addressed alongside other focus areas, or as a discrete focus area. Students should be provided with structured and unstructured opportunities to demonstrate their responses to the communication of others, and develop social routines and skills required for everyday life. Challenge is provided when skills are demonstrated in increasingly unfamiliar contexts.

For most students, communication will include speaking and listening skills. Students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, may use signing, speaking or both. Students who use other forms of communication to supplement or replace speech content should be taught through speaking and listening experiences, where appropriate, and in combination with the student’s preferred communication form.

Strategies to address the content include:

    • regular opportunities for structured conversations with teachers, other adults and peers, including through targeted small group work, using open-ended questions to extend interactions
    • reminding students, where appropriate, to speak audibly, including articulating words clearly
    • acknowledging students’ demonstration of listening skills
    • encouraging students to expand on their sentences and ideas
    • asking students to summarise information communicated to them, including posing questions to check for understanding
    • explaining and demonstrating the subtleties of intonation, stress and pace when speaking
    • recasting the same content of a student’s speech by adding new or different grammar, or information to help comprehension
    • explicitly teaching subject vocabulary that may be unfamiliar to students.

How do I assess this focus area?

Students should be assessed against the Life Skills outcomes selected for study through the collaborative curriculum planning process. Outcomes can be assessed individually or in combination with other Life Skills outcomes. Assessment opportunities should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate to achieve success. Student progress can be observed when they are communicating in everyday contexts.

Students may require adjustments in order to engage with and respond to the communication of others.

Further information about assessing English Life Skills outcomes can be found here.

What is Expressing ideas and composing texts?

This focus area develops the skills and strategies that students should demonstrate when composing texts for everyday purposes, and for specific audiences and purposes. It enables students to develop strategies to plan, compose and reflect on their own compositions.

These skills and strategies are developed through exploring: the functional components of writing, representing and speaking; the stylistic elements that shape meaning in the creation of texts in a wide range of forms, media and modes, including written, aural, visual and multimodal texts; and the process of composition, including planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting.

For students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, spoken texts may be created through signing, speaking or both. For students who use other forms of communication to supplement or replace speech, spoken texts may be developed using the student’s preferred communication form(s).

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers can address the outcomes and content in this focus area by designing learning experiences that require students to express their ideas through composing texts in a range of modes, including multimodal responses. The content provides opportunities for engaging with the process of composition, including planning, monitoring, revising and reflecting. Stylistic elements of students’ preferred communication form(s) could be specifically addressed.

Strategies to address the content include:

    • modelling sentence construction using think-aloud, and allowing students to practise saying sentences orally
    • using word banks to support students’ language choices when writing
    • modelling and encouraging the use of graphic organisers when planning to compose a text
    • selecting activities that allow students to manipulate sentence fragments, scrambled sentences and run-on sentences, in order to develop an understanding of a complete sentence
    • encouraging students to deepen their responses to stimuli, to provide them with ideas for developing interesting topic sentences
    • ensuring the use of explicit strategy instruction, with focus on planning, sequencing, composing, revising, editing and publishing texts.

How do I assess this focus area?

Students should be assessed against the Life Skills outcomes selected for study through the collaborative curriculum planning process. Outcomes can be assessed individually or in combination with other Life Skills outcomes. Assessment opportunities should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate to achieve success. Student progress can be observed whenever they are expressing ideas or composing texts.

Students may require adjustments in order to express ideas and compose texts.

Further information about assessing English Life Skills outcomes can be found here.

What is Reading, viewing and listening to texts?

This focus area develops the skills of reading, viewing and listening to texts. These skills and strategies assist students in developing their ability to understand and make meaning from a range of texts. They learn to reflect on their reading, viewing and listening, and develop into active and independent learners.

This focus area details how students can engage with texts for challenge, interest, and enjoyment. This is important for students as they develop and broaden their vocabulary, and their understanding of the world.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

The outcomes in this focus area are addressed when students engage with texts in both familiar and unfamiliar contexts. Teaching and learning opportunities which draw from a diverse range of texts can assist students to broaden and develop their language skills. Where appropriate, students should be provided with opportunities to engage with prose, poetry, film and drama in a range of forms, including visual, spoken, multimodal and digital texts. Texts selected should provide an appropriate level of challenge and be accessible for all students. The study of selected extracts of a text, the extended study of specific texts, or the independent reading of a text, can be used to address the English 7–10 Life Skills outcomes. The English 7–10 Text Requirements provide further advice about selecting texts to meet the needs of diverse learners.

Strategies to address the content include:

    • selecting texts that students are able to perform, including rhythmical, rhetorical, or interactive texts, such as poetry, song lyrics, chants, rhymes, plays, monologues, dialogues and letters
    • selecting texts from a variety of genres that offer cultural or personal links to the individual student
    • identifying a goal or purpose for engaging with a text, and determining the relevance of a text for a particular task
    • building topic knowledge prior to engaging with a selected text
    • explaining how sentence openers can help to identify what a sentence is about
    • modelling how to identify key words in a text that support understanding
    • identifying and describing a specific comprehension strategy and modelling this strategy when reading aloud to students, for example, by using think-aloud prompts, or by recording information using visual tools, such as charts or tables
    • guided reading where students can apply a specific strategy, for example, with teacher modelling, followed by students reading in pairs, and then independently
    • reflecting with students by discussing how the strategy helps to understand a text
    • providing opportunities for students to reflect on their personal reading goals and reading experiences
    • providing opportunities for students to discuss texts and/or language features that they enjoy.

How do I assess this focus area?

Students should be assessed against the Life Skills outcomes selected for study through the collaborative curriculum planning process. Outcomes can be assessed individually or in combination with other Life Skills outcomes. Assessment opportunities should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate to achieve success. Student progress can be observed whenever they are reading, viewing or listening to texts.

Students may require adjustments in order to access and respond to texts.

Further information about assessing English Life Skills outcomes can be found here.

What is Understanding and responding to texts?

This focus area develops students’ knowledge and understanding of texts. Students learn to understand and respond to texts by exploring how language and visual forms and features, aesthetic qualities, voice, and structural components of texts represent ideas and values. They develop skills to find meaning in a range of texts, and build an understanding of how language and textual elements shape texts, including the purpose of a text, and how characters are created. They also build an understanding of how texts can be understood in relation to one another.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas, and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

The outcomes in this focus area are addressed when students are supported to consider the different ways that texts can express experiences and ideas. Students should be supported to personally respond to these experiences and ideas using their preferred communication form(s).

Teachers can design learning experiences that require students to consider how the forms and features of texts shape the representation of ideas and values, and how meaning is constructed in the texts of others, and their own texts. Students should also be encouraged to make connections between texts.

Strategies to address the content include:

    • comparing written and spoken language to explore the differences in language and features
    • identifying words that express tone or mood
    • identifying examples of imagery and what they imply
    • exploring what different characters know, feel and understand in a text, and why
    • discussing how words can influence an emotional response from the responder (eg towards characters in a narrative)
    • providing opportunities to present justified opinions of a text or character
    • highlighting lexical cohesive devices in texts
    • identifying the author and the author’s perspective
    • discussing what makes something a fact or an opinion, and why a perspective might or might not be authoritative
    • discussing how different types of verbs used by authors control meaning
    • identifying the cultural and social influence of the author.

How do I assess this focus area?

Students should be assessed against the Life Skills outcomes selected for study through the collaborative curriculum planning process. Outcomes can be assessed individually or in combination with other Life Skills outcomes. Assessment opportunities should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate to achieve success. Student progress can be observed whenever they are understanding or responding to texts.

Students may require adjustments in order to access and respond to texts.

Further information about assessing English Life Skills outcomes can be found here.

What is Reading, viewing and listening to texts?

Students read, view and listen to texts through comprehension, inference and analysis. These skills and strategies, having been developed in earlier stages, are now refined to a more sophisticated level to support progression through Stage 5 and into Stage 6. This may include drawing on experiences and aspects of texts, engaging deeply with texts, and supporting student autonomy when engaging with texts. It is important that students have a breadth of reading experiences of complex texts in Stage 5 to assist them to produce high quality writing.

Students develop their metacognitive skills to reflect on reading and become independent readers and learners.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers should provide students with a broad range of opportunities to engage with texts from a variety of forms, media and technologies, such as through the study of selected extracts of a text, the extended study of specific texts or sustained independent reading. Texts should be selected in accordance with the 7–10 text requirements, provide an appropriate level of challenge and be accessible for all students.

How do I assess this focus area?

The outcome for this focus area should be assessed in conjunction with outcomes from other focus areas. This assessment should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate.

Using the content, teachers can assess students’ development of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills required for reading, viewing and listening to texts. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access and respond to texts.

Students' progress can be observed when they express an understanding of texts with which they have engaged. Understanding can be expressed in many forms, including through home languages or dialects.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may benefit from explicit teaching of vocabulary, cultural references and context, as well as having access to glossaries and transcripts when reading, viewing and listening to texts. Modelling pace, tone and pronunciation, and providing frequent opportunities to practise reading aloud, can support development of students’ reading fluency. Students may benefit from using their home language(s) and/or dialect(s) when reading for interest and enjoyment and when reflecting on the experience of reading.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in Listening and Reading/viewing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Reading, viewing and listening to texts.

Teachers can use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding level 7 and Oral interaction level 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
What is Understanding and responding to texts?

As the central focus of their learning in English, students develop their knowledge and understanding of texts in order to compose responses in a range of modes and for a range of contexts, purposes and audiences.

Students refine the skills and strategies, developed in earlier stages, that relate to the study of textual forms and features, aesthetic qualities, voice, and how the structural components of texts represent a wide range of ideas and values. They broaden their understanding of how texts from different historical, social and cultural contexts may challenge or reflect the values and perspectives of groups and individuals. They also deeply explore how texts can be understood in relation to one another.

How do I address this focus area?

The content in this focus area is interrelated with content from other focus areas and teachers should plan to address combinations of content from across all focus areas, as appropriate.

Teachers should design learning experiences that require students to consider how forms and features of texts shape the representation of ideas and values, and connections and relationships, and how meaning is determined in the texts of others and their own texts.

How do I assess this focus area?

The outcomes for this focus area should be assessed in conjunction with outcomes from other focus areas. This assessment should clearly identify the specific knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate.

Using the content, teachers can assess students’ development of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills required for understanding and responding to texts. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access and respond to texts.

Students' progress can be observed when they are engaging with the ideas, perspectives and values in texts, and how these are communicated and understood. Students can demonstrate their understanding through written, spoken, visual and multimodal responses. Where the mode of response has been prescribed by the teacher, this should not preclude students from using their preferred communication form(s). Assessment of this focus area should consider the texts of others and students’ own texts.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Explicit pre-teaching of cultural contexts and vocabulary will provide access for students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) to engage with the ideas, perspectives and values represented in texts. Some students may not have been exposed to a range of text types and so modelling of language forms and features and explicit scaffolding of responses will support these students when responding to and/or demonstrating their understanding of texts. Students will also benefit from using their home language(s) and/or dialect(s) when planning their written tasks and when reflecting on their work.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Understanding and responding to texts A.

Teachers can use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and responding level 7, Writing level 7 and Oral interaction level 8 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
In Stage 1, teachers engage students in structured and deep conversations about a wide range of literature that they read aloud to them. These conversations should move beyond traditional who, what, when and where questions to build students’ deeper understanding that goes beyond the print on the page and explores the different levels of meaning in the text. Teaching about context, narrative, character, imagery perspective and argument through strategic choice and use of language, images, text structure and other conventions provides students with opportunities to think critically about textual representations of the world.

Where reading aloud is not accessible for students, they should be read to using their preferred communication form(s).

Students can benefit from their teacher reading literature that is more complex in structure, language and visual elements than the texts students may read independently.

Teachers select literature that:

  • introduces new and unfamiliar contexts and experiences
  • represents a range of cultural, linguistic and social perspectives
  • is rich in language and visual features
  • merits multiple readings for the purposes of deep study
  • provides a variety of models of language, and text structures and features
  • includes diversity of characters while avoiding stereotypical representations of culture.

Reading widely to students should be part of a robust range of classroom activities across learning areas. It should occur daily, wherever possible. By using a wide range of literature, the teaching of reading can be integrated with the teaching of writing.

Through understanding and responding to literature, students can:

  • build disciplinary and world knowledge
  • broaden their vocabulary and grammar.

When teachers read literature to students, the students experience effective reading fluency. Through rich discussions about texts, students develop their oral language skills and enhance their understanding of the text.

Rich talk about literature

Students should be provided with opportunities to respond to literature by engaging them in rich talk about the texts that they read aloud. To extend students and provide opportunities for critical and creative thinking, rich talk can focus on increasingly complex and abstract vocabulary and ideas.

During rich talk, students are provided with opportunities to:

  • use their oral vocabulary to retell story events
  • share key ideas in an information text
  • identify how words and images work together within a text to convey a particular message, position the reader/viewer and contribute to their engagement
  • discuss how authors/illustrators make specific choices about language forms, features and structures to suit their purpose, audience and context.

Rich talk can be facilitated through a literature or yarning circle. A yarning circle can be held in a designated school space, or the concept can be applied in the classroom context. The teacher can also use these opportunities to select target words from the texts for explicit vocabulary instruction.

When using rich talk, it is important to ensure all students can participate. Some students with disability communicate through a variety of verbal or nonverbal communication techniques or systems. It is important that students are supported to participate in discussions about texts using their preferred communication form(s).

Reading to write

Mentor texts offer models of well-structured and well-presented written and multimodal fiction and non-fiction literature for a wide range of purposes and audiences. They can provide the stimulus for students to create their own text through written and/or digital means.

Further support

Additional opportunities for guided and independent practice may be required, in the classroom or through specific interventions. Early intervention to support the development of literacy skills is essential. Decisions about adjustments for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) will benefit from sharing narratives from their home language(s) or dialect(s).

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Listening, Speaking, Reading/viewing and Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Understanding and responding to literature.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Reading and Responding level 3 and 4, Writing level 3 and Oral interaction level 5 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners within this focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
What are print conventions?

Print conventions are understandings about how print works in texts and the environment. Knowing how print works in English is an essential part of learning to read and write.

These conventions provide students with a basic framework for organising and presenting ideas. A student can use these conventions with other forms of reading and writing knowledge, such as phonic knowledge, spelling and handwriting.

Print conventions provide guidance in identifying the match between spoken and written words. Skilled readers and writers use their knowledge of print conventions to:

  • efficiently navigate their way around a text when reading
  • create written texts with spaces between words.

Students start school with varying levels of knowledge about print conventions in English. Some students may know about print but have not developed a sophisticated understanding of print conventions. Once students have developed an understanding of print conventions, further teaching is not required.

Supporting students learning English as an additional language or dialect

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may have already developed ideas about how print works based on their first language. Languages use different print conventions. For example:

  • In Arabic, print travels from right to left across the page.
  • In Mandarin, readers begin reading at what an English reader might consider to be the back of the book.

Identifying a student’s proficiency in the Writing modes of the EAL/D Learning Progression can support teachers to understand the student’s language needs in relation to Print conventions.

Teachers can also use the ESL Scales to assess students’ current levels of English language proficiency. The skills and understandings described in the ESL Scales for Writing level 1 can be used to support English language learning for EAL/D learners in this focus area.

Teaching print conventions

Explicit and systematic teaching of print conventions involves the deliberate explanation and demonstration of how print works in a planned and sequential way.

Instruction for print conventions is an important component of early literacy learning that should not be overlooked. It should focus on showing students:

  • what these conventional patterns are
  • how they are used in a range of print-based texts
  • how to apply them to help fluent reading and comprehension
  • how to apply them in creating their own texts.

web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Content
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Assessment is used to analyse and interpret the knowledge, understanding and skills that students demonstrate throughout the learning process. Assessment provides information about student learning and achievement at a point in time and the progress students have made.

Assessment is most effective when it is an integral part of teaching and learning. The primary role of assessment is to identify where students are in their learning so that teaching can be adapted to target student needs, and progress can be monitored over time.

Schools use syllabuses, assessment and reporting materials and Assessment Certification and Examination (ACE) requirements to develop school-based assessment programs.

Assessment involves:

  •  identifying where students are in their learning
  •  ongoing monitoring of student progress in relation to the syllabus
  •  providing feedback about student progress to determine the next steps in learning.

Effective school-based assessment:

  • enables students to demonstrate what they know, understand and can do
  • is inclusive of, and accessible for, all students
  • is valid: there is clear alignment between the syllabus, the assessment activity and the criteria used to assess
  • identifies strengths, misunderstandings and skills not yet mastered
  • enables timely and relevant feedback about learning progress
  • provides opportunities for students to reflect on feedback
  • is regular, purposeful and integrated throughout teaching and learning
  • informs goal setting for learning and teaching.

Teachers should evaluate the effectiveness of their assessment approaches regularly to ensure they are fit for purpose. Reviewing student work in relation to assessment activities can provide useful information for decision-making.

Decisions teachers make about teaching, learning and assessment include:

  • what outcomes will be assessed in relation to the content that has been taught
  • why assessment will occur at a point in time and for what purpose
  • how information about student learning will be gathered and what approach will be used
  • how the information will be used, including to provide feedback, and to determine student progress and achievement
  • what next steps will inform future teaching and learning.

Standards-referenced assessment

Standards-referenced assessment refers to the process of interpreting information about student learning in relation to standards. It is used to compare student performance to a standard with objective criteria rather than to the performance of other students. Standards-referenced assessment can provide meaningful feedback about student achievement and support consistent assessment and reporting.

What are standards?

A standards-referenced approach is used to assess and report student achievement in NSW. This approach comprises 2 components:

  • syllabus outcomes and content describe what students are expected to learn
  • how well students demonstrate achievement is described in performance standards such as the Common Grade Scale.

Syllabus outcomes are used by teachers to:

  • plan and develop learning and assessment opportunities in relation to content
  • assess student progress and achievement in relation to intended learning
  • report student progress and achievement at key points in time.

Performance standards used to report student achievement in NSW include:

  • Common Grade Scale (Years 1 to 10)
  • Stage 5 Course Performance Descriptors (end of Year 10)
  • Common Grade Scale for preliminary courses (Year 11)
  • HSC Performance Band Descriptions (Year 12)
  • achievement level descriptions (Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1, and Numeracy).

It is not a requirement for student reports in Early Stage 1 to refer to a performance standard such as a grade scale. More information on standards-referenced reporting is available in Reporting and using grades.

Inclusive assessment

Approaches to assessment should be inclusive of all students. Assessment design should consider the ways students engage in the activity, how information is presented and accessed, and the different ways that students can demonstrate their understanding. Inclusive assessment means ensuring all students are able to demonstrate their learning.

Inclusive assessment considers the following:

  • How students engage:
    • developing accessible learning goals and criteria
    • integrating student choice, for example allowing students to choose topics or contexts in which they demonstrate learning
    • simulating real-life contexts that have explicit relevance to students.
  • How information is presented and accessed, including:
    • resources and/or stimulus material that is presented across a range of modes and that include accessibility options
    • both digital and non-digital resources.
  • How students respond:
    • using self-paced activities that support students to demonstrate learning without time constraints
    • providing opportunities for students to make choices about how they communicate their learning
    • providing opportunities to challenge and/or extend students within their level of understanding.

Adjustments for students with disability

It is a requirement under the Disability Standards for Education 2005 for schools to ensure that assessment tasks are accessible to students with disability. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access assessment activities and tasks and to demonstrate their learning. In some cases, this may mean providing an alternative assessment activity. Schools are responsible for any decisions made at school level to offer adjustments to assessment activities and tasks, including in-school tests. Decisions regarding adjustments should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning. 

Related information

  • ACE Rules
  • Formative assessment
  • Summative assessment
  • Evidence and feedback
  • Reporting and using grades
  • Assessment in Stage 6

Checking grades involves reviewing the history of grades allocated by a school to analyse patterns and clarify grading decisions.

When making comparisons, teachers should ensure their grading decisions are based on all available assessment information referenced by relevant grade scales or performance descriptors and published standards.

Schools can use the Grade History Function in Schools Online or the Results Analysis Package to view the grades they have allocated in each course.

Schools can monitor their grade patterns by comparing them to other available data about the performance of students at their school. This will enable schools to have confidence that the grades they intend to allocate are consistent with what they expected from a particular cohort or group of students completing a course.

Principals are accountable for the pattern of grades allocated by their school at the end of Stage 5 and Year 11 courses (except Life Skills and VET) and Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC. Principals (or their delegates) need to confirm that grades are consistent with published standards when they are submitted.

Related information

  • Assessment in Stage 6
